WAL-CLM-DDDL-000247.question: How much phosphorus is in the human body and where is it stored?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000247.answer_short: The body holds about 800 grams of phosphorus — just under two pounds — with 700 grams locked in the bones and teeth as insoluble calcium phosphate.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000248.subject: phosphorus
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000248.question: Do B vitamins need phosphorus to work?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000248.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says B-complex vitamins only function as coenzymes for intracellular metabolism when they are combined with phosphorus.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000249.subject: phosphorus
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000249.question: How much phosphorus do we eat and how well is it absorbed?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000249.answer_short: Adults eat 1,000-1,500 mg of phosphorus a day, but absorb only 3-5% of metallic phosphorus, 40-50% of chelated forms, and up to 98% of organically bound colloidal phosphorus.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000250.subject: phosphorus
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000250.question: Which foods have too much phosphorus compared to calcium?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000250.answer_short: All the basic foods are lopsided — grain 1:8, red meat and fish 1:12, carbonated drinks 1:8, and organ meat as extreme as 1:44 calcium to phosphorus.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000251.subject: phosphorus
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000251.question: Does phosphorus in grains block absorption of other minerals?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000251.answer_short: Yes — phosphorus in grains occurs as phytates, and phytic acid in unleavened bread binds calcium, iron, zinc and other minerals, lowering their absorption.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000252.subject: phosphorus
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000252.question: What happens if you are deficient in phosphorus?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000252.answer_short: Phosphorus deficiency is widespread and ultimately fatal, collapsing ATP synthesis into complete metabolic energy failure with neuromuscular, skeletal, blood and kidney disease.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000253.subject: phosphorus
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000253.question: Do Americans get too much phosphorus?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000253.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says most American diets run 15 to 20 parts phosphorus to 1 part calcium, the reverse of the healthy 2:1 calcium-to-phosphorus ratio.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000254.subject: phosphorus
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000254.question: Why do phosphorus-deficient animals chew on bones and wood?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000254.answer_short: A 'phosphate appetite' drives phosphorus-deficient cattle to anxiously search pastures for discarded bones (osteophagia) and to gnaw on wood and each other's horns.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000255.subject: sulfur
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000255.question: Which proteins in the body contain sulfur?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000255.answer_short: Sulfur is built into hemoglobin, hormones such as insulin and the adrenal cortical hormones, enzymes, and antibodies.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000256.subject: sulfur
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000256.question: Why are my fingernails brittle?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000256.answer_short: Wallach reads brittle fingernails as a sign of sulfur amino acid and protein deficiency.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000257.subject: sulfur
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000257.question: Why do farts smell like rotten eggs?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000257.answer_short: Wallach says the rotten-egg smell is sulfur released when unabsorbed proteins reach the colon and are fermented by bowel organisms.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000258.subject: sulfur
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000258.question: Can sulfur treat scabies?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000258.answer_short: For scabies, Wallach recommends a 5-10% sulfur ointment for infants, in place of the adult chemical treatments, to avoid potential neurotoxicity.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000259.subject: sulfur
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000259.question: What are the symptoms of sulfur deficiency?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000259.answer_short: Wallach says a sulfur deficiency produces degenerative arthritis and cartilage breakdown, weakened ligaments and tendons, lupus, sickle cell anemia, and other collagen diseases.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000260.subject: sulfur
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000260.question: Is lupus caused by a nutritional deficiency?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000260.answer_short: Wallach argues lupus features multiple mineral deficiencies of sulfur, copper, and selenium, and that its autoimmune damage is a result of the disease, not its cause.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000261.subject: chloride
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000261.question: What is Chloride?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000261.answer_short: Chloride is an essential mineral and one of the body's three key electrolytes; Wallach says its most important job is supplying the raw material your stomach uses to make hydrochloric acid.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000262.subject: chloride
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000262.question: What does chloride actually do in the body?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000262.answer_short: Chloride is the raw material your stomach uses to make hydrochloric acid; it is essential to all living things and activates numerous enzymes.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000263.subject: chloride
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000263.question: How much of the body is chloride, and what does it do with sodium and potassium?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000263.answer_short: Chlorine makes up three percent of the body's total mineral content and works with sodium and potassium as one of three indispensable electrolytes.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000264.subject: chloride
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000264.question: What does the sweat test measure and is it really specific to cystic fibrosis?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000264.answer_short: It measures sodium, chloride, and potassium in sweat; Wallach says it is nonspecific, turning positive in 17 different diseases.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000265.subject: chloride
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000265.question: Can a low-salt diet cause low stomach acid?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000265.answer_short: Yes—Wallach says sodium chloride is the raw material for stomach acid, so a salt-restricted diet makes achlorhydria more likely.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000320.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000320.question: How much salt do you lose when you sweat?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000320.answer_short: Wallach says soldiers sweating in the desert can lose up to 70 to 100 grams of salt per day — enough that sodium loss historically killed troops.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000321.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000321.question: What does sodium do in the body?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000321.answer_short: Sodium is one of the three indispensable electrolytes and, with chloride and potassium, runs the body's water balance, osmotic and acid-base equilibrium, and nerve and muscle function.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000322.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000322.question: Why do I crave salt?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000322.answer_short: Salt hunger is one of the oldest and most basic cravings of living things, and plant-eaters crave it far more than meat-eaters because grains, vegetables and fruit contain little or no natural salt.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000323.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000323.question: Can a low-salt diet cause a vitamin B12 deficiency?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000323.answer_short: Yes, too little salt lowers stomach acid, which stops the intrinsic factor from working, so vitamin B12 cannot be absorbed.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000324.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000324.question: How much salt do you actually need each day?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000324.answer_short: Wallach puts the average human salt requirement at about six to ten grams per day — roughly 0.5% of the dry weight of the daily diet.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000325.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000325.question: Can cutting back on salt cause anemia or low iron?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000325.answer_short: Yes, salt-restricted diets lower stomach acid, and that impaired stomach acid is one of Wallach's listed causes of iron deficiency.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000326.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000326.question: Can restricting salt cause thyroid problems or goiter?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000326.answer_short: Yes, Wallach says Americans restricting their salt on doctors' orders has driven goiter and hypothyroidism to epidemic levels.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000327.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000327.question: What happens if you don't get enough sodium?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000327.answer_short: Sodium deficiency strikes mainly in heat and heavy sweating, and low-sodium infant formulas have caused fatal 'water intoxication' with brain swelling; the treatment is water and salt.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000328.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000328.question: Is salt actually bad for you?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000328.answer_short: No — Wallach teaches that salt is not intrinsically harmful; its only real danger is that it can trick the body into thinking it already has enough minerals.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000329.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000329.question: Do low-salt diets actually help high blood pressure?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000329.answer_short: Wallach says no — he claims there is not a single double-blind study showing any benefit from a salt-restricted or low-sodium diet.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000330.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000330.question: If salt causes high blood pressure, why don't farm animals get it?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000330.answer_short: Wallach points out that livestock eat all the salt they want from salt blocks yet never develop high blood pressure or stroke.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000331.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000331.question: Can your body actually know when it needs salt?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000331.answer_short: Wallach cites a 1940 case of a boy whose intense salt craving kept his undiagnosed Addison's disease at bay — he died 48 hours after doctors restricted his salt.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000332.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000332.question: Is salt really the cause of high blood pressure?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000332.answer_short: No, Wallach argues that the 'salt sensitivity' seen in hypertension is actually driven by low calcium and potassium intake, not by salt itself.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000333.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000333.question: Why was salt so valuable in ancient times?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000333.answer_short: Wallach says salt was so essential a necessity of life that people in salt-poor Africa gave up everything they owned — even their wives and children — to obtain it, and that African tribesmen said, 'He who has salt has war.'

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000334.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000334.question: Why is salt connected to the word 'salary'?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000334.answer_short: Roman soldiers were partly paid in a salt ration called a 'salarium' — the origin of the word 'salary' and the phrase 'worth their salt.'

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000335.subject: phosphorus
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000335.question: What causes low blood phosphorus?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000335.answer_short: Low blood phosphorus (hypophosphatemia) results from IV glucose or TPN without phosphorus, excessive antacids, hyperparathyroidism, diuretics, sweating from exercise, and alcoholism.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000336.subject: phosphorus
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000336.question: Do vegetarians get enough phosphorus?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000336.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says vegetarians and vegans who don't supplement with minerals rarely have a phosphorus deficiency (unless they have chronic gluten intolerance from heavy whole-grain consumption), though because of their high phytic-acid intake they always have other mineral deficiencies, such as calcium, copper, chromium, vanadium, lithium and zinc, unless they supplement.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000337.subject: phosphorus
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000337.question: How did phosphorus get its name?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000337.answer_short: In 1669 the German alchemist Hennig Brandt heated human urine with beach sand; the glowing white residue he named 'phosphorus', Greek for 'I bear light.'

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000338.subject: sulfur
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000338.question: What did alchemists believe about sulfur?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000338.answer_short: Alchemists held that all metals were made of sulphur and mercury, and that the proportions of each decided whether a metal became gold, silver, copper, or tin.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000339.subject: chloride
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000339.question: Why is chlorine put in drinking water?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000339.answer_short: Since a 1918 U.S. decree, chlorine has disinfected public water—Wallach notes it kills E. coli far better than bromine or iodine.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000340.subject: chloride
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000340.question: Why is chlorine called chlorine, and what does the word mean?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000340.answer_short: Sir Humphry Davy named it in 1810 from the Greek 'chloros,' meaning green-yellow.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000059.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000059.question: Why does the body need salt?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000059.answer_short: Salt is the raw material for stomach acid, which digests food, absorbs minerals, and activates pepsin and B12's intrinsic factor.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000060.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000060.question: What happens if you don't eat enough salt?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000060.answer_short: Wallach says restricting salt causes heat intolerance, digestive problems like GERD, and low stomach acid that raises disease risk.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000061.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000061.question: Does salt cause high blood pressure?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000061.answer_short: No — Wallach says salt does not cause high blood pressure, and restricting it actually shortens your life.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000062.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000062.question: Is a low-salt diet actually bad for your heart?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000062.answer_short: Yes — Wallach cites a 1997 Sodium Task Force report that heavy salt-restrictors had 600% more heart attacks.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000063.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000063.question: Why do the Japanese eat so much salt but have less heart disease?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000063.answer_short: Wallach notes the Japanese ate 15 grams of salt a day yet had 85% less cardiovascular disease and hypertension than Americans.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000064.subject: phosphorus
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000064.question: Can mineral deficiency cause binge eating and obesity?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000064.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says iron and phosphorus deficiencies occurring together trigger an almost psychotic binge-eating and soft-drink rampage that results in morbid obesity.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000065.subject: chloride
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000065.question: Is a low-salt diet actually bad for you?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000065.answer_short: Wallach says salt deficiency is common and is often caused by doctors wrongly telling patients to cut salt—the profession, he says, thinks humans are dumber than cows.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000372.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000372.question: What is sodium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000372.answer_short: Sodium is a soft, highly reactive silvery metal and the sixth most abundant element in the earth's crust, known best as sodium chloride — common table salt. Wallach treats it as an essential macro-mineral and one of the body's three indispensable electrolytes.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000373.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000373.question: What is sodium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000373.answer_short: Sodium is a highly reactive, soft silvery metal, light enough to float on water and the sixth most abundant element in the earth's crust.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000374.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000374.question: Why do animals crave salt and need salt licks?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000374.answer_short: Animals have an instinctive salt hunger, so farmers use salt blocks (at least 85% sodium chloride) to make them consume trace minerals.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000375.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000375.question: Where does table salt come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000375.answer_short: Wallach says table salt (sodium chloride) is mined from ancient salt mines on every continent, and seawater holds a quarter pound of salt per gallon.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000376.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000376.question: Is processed table salt as good as natural salt?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000376.answer_short: No — unprocessed salt once carried trace minerals and rare earths, while modern processed salt fools the body into thinking it is getting minerals.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000377.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000377.question: Who discovered sodium and where does its name come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000377.answer_short: Sir Humphry Davy isolated sodium in 1807; the name comes from 'soda,' from the Latin 'sodanum,' an ancient Roman headache remedy.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000378.subject: phosphorus
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000378.question: Who discovered phosphorus?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000378.answer_short: The German physician Hennig Brand discovered phosphorus in 1669 by distilling boiled-down urine, producing a substance that glowed in the dark.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000379.subject: sulfur
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000379.question: What is sulfur?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000379.answer_short: In Wallach's framework sulfur is one of the 60 essential minerals — a structural atom built into most proteins through the sulfur amino acids cystine, cysteine, and methionine.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000380.subject: sulfur
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000380.question: What does sulfur do in the body?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000380.answer_short: Sulfur is a structural atom in most proteins, carried by the sulfur amino acids cystine, cysteine, and methionine, and it is essential to glutathione.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000381.subject: sulfur
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000381.question: Where is sulfur stored in the body?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000381.answer_short: Sulfur concentrates in cartilage, tendons, keratin, skin, intervertebral discs, hair, and nails, and is lowest in the bones.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000382.subject: sulfur
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000382.question: Do sulfur amino acids help you live longer?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000382.answer_short: Wallach counts the sulfur-bearing amino acids among the antioxidants shown to significantly extend the average lifespan of a population.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000514.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-LETS-000514.question: What does sodium do in the body?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000514.answer_short: Sodium is an essential macro-mineral that maintains acid-base balance, fluid pressure in the blood and tissues, and neuromuscular function.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000515.subject: phosphorus
WAL-CLM-LETS-000515.question: What is a normal phosphorus level on a blood test?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000515.answer_short: Wallach gives a normal blood phosphorus range of 3.1–4.5 mg%, kept within narrow limits by parathyroid hormone.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000516.subject: chloride
WAL-CLM-LETS-000516.question: What is a normal chloride level in the blood?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000516.answer_short: Wallach gives a normal blood chloride range of 95–110 mEq/L; low levels point to diarrhea, infection, diabetes, or weak adrenals.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000367.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000367.question: Does eating salt make you lose calcium?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000367.answer_short: Yes — diets heavy in salt raise the body's calcium 'cost,' pushing urinary calcium loss up (from 96 to 148 mg a day when food was heavily salted).

WAL-CLM-RARE-000368.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000368.question: Do pregnant women need more salt?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000368.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says pregnancy requires a net increase in salt to keep water in the blood vessels, so salty-food cravings make sense.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000369.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000369.question: Do vegetarians need more salt?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000369.answer_short: Yes — Wallach notes grains and green foods are very low in sodium, so vegetarians need a significant salt supplement, as Gandhi argued for India.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000370.subject: sulfur
WAL-CLM-RARE-000370.question: Why does hair need sulfur?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000370.answer_short: Hair keratin contains cystine, a sulfur amino acid, and perms, bleaches, dyes, and depilatories significantly decrease its cystine levels, changing the hair's physical characteristics and its ability to bind trace minerals.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000371.subject: sulfur
WAL-CLM-RARE-000371.question: What foods are high in sulfur?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000371.answer_short: Wallach says organ meats such as liver and kidney can significantly increase the availability of sulfur, along with selenium, cobalt, molybdenum, and zinc.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000372.subject: sulfur
WAL-CLM-RARE-000372.question: Is sulfur an essential mineral the body needs?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000372.answer_short: Yes—Wallach counts sulphur among the 60 essential elements, metals and minerals the body must obtain.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000373.subject: chloride
WAL-CLM-RARE-000373.question: Where is chlorine found in nature?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000373.answer_short: Wallach reports chlorine spread across rocks, soils, and water — most concentrated in sea water, and in land animals highest in hair and skin.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000374.subject: chloride
WAL-CLM-RARE-000374.question: What do high chloride levels in a hair mineral analysis mean?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000374.answer_short: Wallach says elevated hair sodium, potassium, and chloride point to an essential fatty acid deficiency, not a true excess.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000375.subject: chloride
WAL-CLM-RARE-000375.question: What causes the body to lose chloride?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000375.answer_short: Wallach ties chloride (as NaCl) loss to conditions like cystic fibrosis and Addison's disease, which disturbs the body's acid-base balance.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000376.subject: chloride
WAL-CLM-RARE-000376.question: Does sodium chloride control water balance in the body?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000376.answer_short: Wallach describes sodium chloride (the cell salt Natrum Mur) as regulating cellular moisture by attracting and distributing water.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000377.subject: chloride
WAL-CLM-RARE-000377.question: Where does the body get chloride?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000377.answer_short: Wallach says ordinary table salt (sodium chloride) is the universal source of chloride ions.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000378.subject: chloride
WAL-CLM-RARE-000378.question: Isn't chlorine a poisonous gas—how can it be essential?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000378.answer_short: Wallach opens his minerals chapter with a quote noting salt joins an explosive metal (sodium) and a lethal gas (chlorine), yet becomes an absolute necessity for life.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000379.subject: chloride
WAL-CLM-RARE-000379.question: Is salt bad for you?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000379.answer_short: Wallach says salt itself is not harmful, contrary to popular belief, though relying on it can fool the body into thinking it's getting minerals.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000380.subject: chloride
WAL-CLM-RARE-000380.question: Who discovered that chloride had medical value?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000380.answer_short: Wallach credits Paracelsus, whose research into minerals and disease led him to the medical value of chloride.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000032.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-LETS-000032.question: What are the symptoms of sodium deficiency?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000032.answer_short: Sodium deficiency can cause abdominal cramps, confusion, dizziness, fatigue, muscular weakness, seizures, and loss of taste, among other signs.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000065.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-LETS-000065.question: How much sodium should you take a day?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000065.answer_short: In his adult Base Line Nutritional Supplement Program table, Wallach lists sodium with three figures: an RDA of 1,100 mg, a supplement level of 3,300 mg, and a daily range of 300 to 3,000 mg.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000033.subject: sodium
WAL-CLM-LETS-000033.question: What happens if you get too much sodium?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000033.answer_short: Sodium excess can cause high blood pressure, edema, congestive heart failure, kidney failure, seizures, and weight gain.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000061.subject: phosphorus
WAL-CLM-LETS-000061.question: How much phosphorus should I supplement?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000061.answer_short: None—phosphorus is the one nutrient in Wallach's Base Line supplement program listed at zero supplemental need.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000206.subject: phosphorus
WAL-CLM-RARE-000206.question: Can too much phosphorus be bad for you?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000206.answer_short: Yes — high phosphorus intake from high-protein diets raises your calcium requirement and can aggravate osteoporosis, arthritis, high blood pressure and loose teeth.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000023.subject: phosphorus
WAL-CLM-LETS-000023.question: What are the symptoms of phosphorus deficiency and too much phosphorus?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000023.answer_short: Deficiency brings anorexia, anxiety, bone pain, fatigue, numbness, pica, and weakness; excess causes calcium malabsorption, loose teeth, osteoporosis, and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000047.subject: chloride
WAL-CLM-LETS-000047.question: How much chloride do I need each day?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000047.answer_short: In his Base Line Nutritional Supplement Program, Wallach lists chloride at a True Supplement Need of 2,500 mg per day (30-day pharmacologic dose 500 to 2,500 mg), against a government RDA of 1,700 mg.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000266.subject: arginine
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000266.question: How much arginine does Wallach recommend for infertility?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000266.answer_short: For infertility, Wallach's protocol includes l-arginine at 500 mg three times a day (t.i.d.).

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000267.subject: arginine
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000267.question: How much arginine is used for cataracts?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000267.answer_short: For cataracts, Wallach's protocol includes l-arginine at 300 mg per day.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000268.subject: arginine
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000268.question: Should I avoid arginine if I get cold sores or herpes?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000268.answer_short: Yes—for herpes, Wallach says to avoid high-arginine foods like chocolate, nuts, seeds and grains, and to eat high-lysine foods instead.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000269.subject: taurine
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000269.question: How much taurine should I take for macular degeneration?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000269.answer_short: Wallach's macular degeneration protocol includes taurine at 2 to 5 grams per day, alongside all 90 essential nutrients.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000270.subject: taurine
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000270.question: Does taurine help with epilepsy or seizures?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000270.answer_short: Wallach lists taurine at 500 mg three times a day among the nutrients indicated for epilepsy.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000271.subject: taurine
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000271.question: Does taurine help with gallstones or gallbladder problems?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000271.answer_short: Wallach's treatment for gallbladder disease and gallstones includes taurine at 500 mg three times a day.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000272.subject: taurine
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000272.question: What is the treatment for absence seizures (petit mal)?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000272.answer_short: Wallach's treatment for absence attacks (petit mal) includes taurine at 500 mg three times a day.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000273.subject: tryptophan
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000273.question: How much tryptophan for depression?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000273.answer_short: For depression, Wallach's program uses dl-phenylalanine, L-tryptophan, and L-tyrosine at 2 grams three times a day each, on top of the base-line supplement program.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000341.subject: arginine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000341.question: What is arginine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000341.answer_short: Arginine is an amino acid Wallach counts among the essentials—required for cell division, wound healing, ammonia excretion, immune support, and the availability of stored hormones.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000342.subject: arginine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000342.question: Why does supplementing with arginine help fuel the cells?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000342.answer_short: Making arginine internally burns ATP, so supplementing it directly frees up more ATP to fuel cell function.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000343.subject: arginine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000343.question: What does arginine do in the body?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000343.answer_short: Arginine is required for cell division, wound healing, ammonia excretion, immune support, and the availability of stored hormones.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000344.subject: arginine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000344.question: Does arginine lower blood pressure and improve circulation?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000344.answer_short: Yes—oral arginine is required to synthesize nitric oxide, and it reduces blood pressure and increases blood flow through obstructed blood vessels.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000345.subject: arginine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000345.question: Can arginine help with tooth pain or sensitivity?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000345.answer_short: An 8% arginine toothpaste gives rapid, effective relief from dental pain by rebuilding a dentin-like layer.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000346.subject: arginine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000346.question: When and how was arginine discovered?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000346.answer_short: Arginine was first isolated in 1886 from a lupin seedling by Swiss chemist Ernst Schultze.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000347.subject: taurine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000347.question: What is taurine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000347.answer_short: Taurine is an amino acid Wallach counts as essential -- a sulfur-based compound that conjugates bile acids, acts as an antioxidant, and is vital to the heart, muscles, eyes, and nervous system.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000348.subject: taurine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000348.question: How does the body make taurine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000348.answer_short: Taurine is synthesized from methionine — Wallach lists it among the compounds methionine is an intermediate in producing.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000349.subject: taurine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000349.question: Can you take too much taurine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000349.answer_short: Wallach warns that doses of taurine above 2 grams a day have been shown to contribute to psoriasis.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000350.subject: taurine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000350.question: Where does the name taurine come from?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000350.answer_short: Taurine is named after the Latin Taurus, meaning bull or ox, because it was first isolated from ox bile in 1827.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000351.subject: tryptophan
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000351.question: What is Tryptophan?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000351.answer_short: Tryptophan is an essential amino acid the body must get from dietary protein; it is a building block for the body's structural enzyme proteins and the raw material it uses to make serotonin, melatonin, and niacin.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000352.subject: tryptophan
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000352.question: What does tryptophan turn into in the body?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000352.answer_short: Tryptophan is a building block of protein and a precursor of serotonin, which the body can convert to melatonin, and it is also used to make niacin.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000353.subject: tryptophan
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000353.question: How much tryptophan equals a milligram of niacin?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000353.answer_short: By convention, 60 mg of tryptophan is considered equivalent to 1 mg of niacin, though measurements found the amount ranged from 39 to 86 mg.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000354.subject: tryptophan
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000354.question: Does phenylalanine affect tryptophan and serotonin?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000354.answer_short: Phenylalanine uses the same transport channel as tryptophan to cross into the brain, so large doses of phenylalanine interfere with serotonin production.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000355.subject: tryptophan
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000355.question: What is 5-HTP used for?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000355.answer_short: 5-HTP, a metabolite of tryptophan, has been suggested as a treatment for seizure disorders and depression; it rapidly crosses into the brain and is converted to serotonin.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000356.subject: tryptophan
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000356.question: Is tryptophan dangerous? What was the 1989 tryptophan outbreak?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000356.answer_short: In 1989 a tryptophan-associated outbreak of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (EMS) caused at least 1,500 cases of permanent disability and at least 37 deaths, traced to a supply of L-tryptophan from a single Japanese manufacturer (Showa Denko KK).

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000357.subject: tryptophan
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000357.question: Who discovered tryptophan and when?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000357.answer_short: Tryptophan was isolated in 1901 by Frederick Hopkins through the hydrolysis of casein, the protein in milk.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000066.subject: arginine
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000066.question: Can arginine raise growth hormone (HGH)?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000066.answer_short: Yes—L-arginine with ornithine can trigger HGH release from the pituitary gland when supplemented in significant doses.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000383.subject: tryptophan
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000383.question: Why do corn-based diets cause pellagra?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000383.answer_short: Corn has very little niacin and its tryptophan is unavailable and can't be absorbed from the intestine, so there is no tryptophan to convert into niacin, causing pellagra.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000384.subject: tryptophan
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000384.question: Why does soaking corn in lye prevent pellagra?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000384.answer_short: Soaking corn in lye and wood ashes overnight lets the alkali free the tryptophan so it can be absorbed, which is why pellagra is rare where corn is prepared this way.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000047.subject: arginine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000047.question: Is arginine used for erectile dysfunction?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000047.answer_short: Yes—arginine is commonly used together with proanthocyanidins or yohimbine to relieve erectile dysfunction.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000058.subject: arginine
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000058.question: Does Wallach consider arginine an essential amino acid?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000058.answer_short: Yes—Wallach adds arginine to the classic essential amino acids, tying its long-term deficiency to cancer and PAD.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000054.subject: taurine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000054.question: What does taurine deficiency cause?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000054.answer_short: A taurine deficiency can produce cataracts and retinal damage; taurine is also needed to maintain skeletal muscle and healthy blood pressure.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000066.subject: taurine
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000066.question: Is taurine an essential amino acid?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000066.answer_short: Wallach adds taurine to the classic list of essential amino acids, saying that over the long haul it helps prevent a specific disease — macular degeneration.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000056.subject: tryptophan
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000056.question: Can gluten intolerance cause depression?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000056.answer_short: Yes; gluten intolerance, lactose intolerance, and fructose malabsorption all reduce tryptophan absorption from the gut, lowering blood tryptophan and producing clinical depression.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000142.subject: tryptophan
WAL-CLM-LETS-000142.question: What does Wallach recommend for anxiety and panic attacks?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000142.answer_short: For anxiety and panic attacks, Wallach's program includes a high dose of L-tryptophan at 10 grams three times a day, plus caffeine and sugar avoidance, chromium, B vitamins, calcium, and magnesium.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000385.subject: cobalt
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000385.question: Where does the name cobalt come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000385.answer_short: From the German 'kobald,' an evil gnome or spirit that miners blamed for their mining accidents.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000139.subject: zinc
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000139.question: How much zinc should I take a day?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000139.answer_short: Wallach's daily supplement chart sets zinc at 15-30 mg per 100 pounds of body weight for adults and children.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000127.subject: boron
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000127.question: How much boron should you take per day?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000127.answer_short: Wallach's daily supplement range for boron is 1 to 6 mg per 100 pounds of body weight.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000123.subject: vitamin-b9
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000123.question: How much folic acid should I take?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000123.answer_short: Wallach's Base Line program lists folic acid with an RDA of 400 mcg, a 'true supplement need' of 1,000 mcg, and a therapeutic (pharmacologic) daily dose of 15 to 20 mg.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000135.subject: molybdenum
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000135.question: What is the recommended daily amount of molybdenum?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000135.answer_short: In Epigenetics, Wallach lists a molybdenum range of 10 to 25 mcg per 100 pounds of body weight for adults and children.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000358.subject: methionine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000358.question: Why is methionine the 'start' amino acid in protein synthesis?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000358.answer_short: Methionine's codon, AUG, doubles as the cell's main 'Start' signal for building a protein, so nearly every protein begins with a methionine.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000359.subject: methionine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000359.question: Can restricting methionine extend lifespan?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000359.answer_short: Wallach cites studies where restricting methionine lengthened lab-animal lifespans; a Nature fruit-fly study found that adding it back restored fertility without cancelling the lifespan gain from calorie restriction.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000360.subject: methionine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000360.question: What does methionine do in plants?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000360.answer_short: In plants, methionine is the raw material for making ethylene (a plant hormone), through a pathway called the Yang Cycle — also known as the methionine cycle.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000361.subject: phenylalanine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000361.question: What is phenylalanine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000361.answer_short: Phenylalanine is one of the nine classic essential amino acids—a nonpolar protein building block the body can't make and must get from food every day.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000362.subject: phenylalanine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000362.question: Is phenylalanine an essential amino acid?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000362.answer_short: Yes—Wallach lists phenylalanine among the nine classic essential amino acids the body cannot make on its own and must be supplied daily from food to prevent deficiency and disease.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000363.subject: phenylalanine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000363.question: When was phenylalanine discovered and who first isolated it?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000363.answer_short: Phenylalanine was first isolated in 1879 by Schulze and Barbieri from yellow lupine, and first synthesized in the lab in 1882 by Erlenmeyer and Lipp.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000364.subject: phenylalanine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000364.question: Is phenylketonuria (PKU) really a genetic disease?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000364.answer_short: Wallach calls PKU—the inability to metabolize phenylalanine—'falsely believed' to be a genetically transmitted disease, and notes its symptoms are prevented simply by avoiding phenylalanine.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000365.subject: phenylalanine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000365.question: Does aspartame (Equal, NutraSweet) contain phenylalanine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000365.answer_short: Yes—aspartame, sold as Equal and NutraSweet, breaks down into phenylalanine, which is why aspartame products carry a 'Contains phenylalanine' warning label.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000366.subject: phenylalanine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000366.question: What is DL-phenylalanine (DLPA) used for?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000366.answer_short: Wallach notes DL-phenylalanine is sold as a nutritional supplement for three purposes: as a sleep aid, as an anti-depressant, and as an analgesic (pain reliever).

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000367.subject: phenylalanine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000367.question: Can large doses of phenylalanine lower serotonin?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000367.answer_short: Yes—phenylalanine shares the same brain-entry transport channel as tryptophan, so in large doses it can crowd tryptophan out and interfere with serotonin production.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000368.subject: tyrosine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000368.question: What is tyrosine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000368.answer_short: Tyrosine is one of 22 amino acids the body uses to build proteins; Wallach adds it to the essential list because a deficiency drives goiter, and it is the raw material for thyroid hormone and key neurotransmitters.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000369.subject: tyrosine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000369.question: Where does the word tyrosine come from?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000369.answer_short: The name tyrosine comes from the Greek word for cheese, because the amino acid was first isolated from cheese in 1846 by the German chemist Justus von Liebig.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000370.subject: tyrosine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000370.question: What does tyrosine do in cell signaling?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000370.answer_short: Tyrosine's phenol group lets it act as a docking point in cell signaling: enzymes called protein kinases attach phosphate groups to it, which switches the activity of the target protein.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000371.subject: tyrosine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000371.question: What role does tyrosine play in plants and photosynthesis?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000371.answer_short: In plants, tyrosine is essential to photosynthesis: inside the chloroplasts it donates an electron to re-charge oxidized chlorophyll during the light reactions.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000372.subject: lysine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000372.question: What is lysine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000372.answer_short: Lysine is an essential amino acid the body can't make and must get daily from food; it drives protein production and, through its derivative allysine, helps build the collagen and elastin that strengthen tissues and blood vessels.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000373.subject: lysine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000373.question: How does the body break down lysine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000373.answer_short: In mammals, lysine is metabolized into acetyl-CoA, a central fuel molecule, in a process that starts with a transamination reaction with alpha-ketoglutarate.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000374.subject: lysine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000374.question: What is the 'lysine contingency' in Jurassic Park?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000374.answer_short: Wallach recounts how the film Jurassic Park gave its cloned dinosaurs a 'lysine contingency', engineering them so they couldn't make their own lysine, keeping them dependent on lysine supplements and unable to survive outside the park.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000375.subject: lysine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000375.question: Why is lysine considered an essential amino acid?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000375.answer_short: Lysine is one of the nine amino acids Wallach lists as classically essential: the body cannot synthesize them, so they must be eaten every day to prevent deficiencies and disease.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000376.subject: leucine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000376.question: What kind of amino acid is leucine and what proteins is it part of?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000376.answer_short: Leucine is a branched-chain, hydrophobic alpha amino acid encoded by six codons; Wallach says it forms a significant part of the ferritin and astacin protein subunits and a class of 'buffer' proteins.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000377.subject: leucine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000377.question: Does leucine help build muscle?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000377.answer_short: Yes—Wallach calls leucine a catalyst for muscle growth and muscle 'insurance,' and says it activates the mTOR kinase, the master switch that regulates cell growth.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000378.subject: leucine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000378.question: Where in the body does leucine work?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000378.answer_short: Leucine has major functions in the liver, fat (adipose) tissue, and muscle; in muscle and fat it is used to synthesize sterols, and its combined use there is greater than in the liver.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000379.subject: leucine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000379.question: Can leucine be toxic?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000379.answer_short: Yes—Wallach warns that leucine toxicity, as in decompensated Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD), produces delirium and neurologic compromise and can be life-threatening.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000380.subject: leucine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000380.question: Can too much leucine cause pellagra?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000380.answer_short: Wallach says excessive leucine intake can produce a clinical pellagra—the classic 'four D's': diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia, and death.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000381.subject: leucine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000381.question: Is leucine an essential amino acid?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000381.answer_short: Yes—Wallach lists leucine among the nine classic essential amino acids the body can't make itself and must get from the diet every day to prevent deficiency and disease.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000382.subject: valine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000382.question: Is valine an essential amino acid?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000382.answer_short: Yes. Wallach lists valine among the nine classic essential amino acids—ones the body can't make on its own, so you must get them from food every day to avoid deficiency and disease.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000383.subject: valine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000383.question: Where does the name valine come from, and who discovered it?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000383.answer_short: Valine — a branched-chain amino acid named after the flowering plant valerian — was first isolated in 1901 from casein (the main protein in milk) by the chemist Emil Fischer.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000384.subject: valine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000384.question: What are the codons for valine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000384.answer_short: Valine (abbreviated Val) is an alpha amino acid encoded by four genetic codons: GUU, GUC, GUA, and GUG.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000385.subject: valine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000385.question: What does valine have to do with sickle cell disease?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000385.answer_short: In sickle-cell disease valine takes the place of glutamic acid in hemoglobin; because valine repels water while glutamic acid attracts it, the hemoglobin becomes more likely to clump together.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000386.subject: histidine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000386.question: Is histidine an essential amino acid?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000386.answer_short: Yes—Wallach lists histidine among the nine classic essential amino acids, which the body can't make and must get from the diet every day to avoid deficiency disease.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000387.subject: histidine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000387.question: Who discovered histidine and when?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000387.answer_short: Histidine was first isolated in 1896 by the German physician Albrecht Kossel, and is one of the 22 amino acids the body uses to build proteins.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000388.subject: histidine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000388.question: How does histidine work in enzymes?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000388.answer_short: Histidine's imidazole side chain binds metals and sits in enzyme catalytic sites, where it pulls a proton off serine, threonine, or cysteine to switch them on as nucleophiles.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000389.subject: isoleucine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000389.question: What is isoleucine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000389.answer_short: Isoleucine is one of the nine classically essential amino acids—an alpha amino acid with a hydrocarbon side chain that makes it hydrophobic, and the body uses it to build protein.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000390.subject: isoleucine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000390.question: Is isoleucine an essential amino acid?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000390.answer_short: Yes—isoleucine is one of nine classically essential amino acids the human body cannot synthesize, so it must be eaten every day to prevent deficiency and disease.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000391.subject: isoleucine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000391.question: Who discovered isoleucine and when?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000391.answer_short: Isoleucine was isolated in 1903 by Felix Ehrlich, a German chemist, who obtained it from hemoglobin.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000392.subject: threonine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000392.question: Is threonine an essential amino acid?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000392.answer_short: Yes—Wallach lists threonine among the nine classic essential amino acids the body can't make itself, so it must be eaten every day to prevent deficiency diseases.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000393.subject: threonine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000393.question: How does the body process and metabolize threonine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000393.answer_short: After it's built into proteins threonine can be tagged by glycosylation and phosphorylation, and it's broken down via threonine dehydrogenase into intermediates like pyruvate, acetyl-CoA, and glycine.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000274.subject: phenylalanine
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000274.question: How much phenylalanine does Wallach recommend for insomnia?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000274.answer_short: For insomnia, Wallach's protocol includes dl-phenylalanine at 250 mg three times a day, along with avoiding caffeine, plus calcium, chromium, l-tryptophan, inositol and niacinamide.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000275.subject: tyrosine
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000275.question: Is tyrosine an essential amino acid?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000275.answer_short: Mainstream science calls tyrosine non-essential, but Wallach adds it to the essential list because, over the long haul, a deficiency causes a specific disease -- goiter.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000276.subject: tyrosine
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000276.question: How does tyrosine relate to the thyroid and goiter?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000276.answer_short: Tyrosine combines with iodine to build the thyroid hormone thyroxin, so a shortage of tyrosine, along with iodine, copper, or molybdenum, is one cause of goiter.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000277.subject: lysine
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000277.question: What foods are high in lysine?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000277.answer_short: Wallach lists meat, potatoes, milk, yeast, fish, chicken, beans, and eggs as high-lysine foods, recommending them (while avoiding high-arginine foods) for people dealing with herpes.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000278.subject: lysine
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000278.question: How much lysine does Wallach recommend for shingles?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000278.answer_short: For shingles, Wallach's treatment of choice includes lysine at 5 grams a day, along with the antivirals Isoprinosin and Ribavirin, vitamin B12, vitamin C to bowel tolerance, vitamin E, and zinc.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000279.subject: valine
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000279.question: What is valine's function in the body?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000279.answer_short: In Wallach's essential-amino-acid chart, valine's function is protein production—it serves as one of the raw building blocks the body uses to make its proteins.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000280.subject: histidine
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000280.question: What does histidine do in the body?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000280.answer_short: In Wallach's amino-acid function table, histidine's job is the formation of histamine — the compound the body releases during allergic reactions and immune responses.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000281.subject: isoleucine
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000281.question: What does isoleucine do in the body?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000281.answer_short: In Wallach's essential amino-acid function table, isoleucine's role is protein production—it serves as a direct building block for the body's proteins.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000282.subject: threonine
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000282.question: What does threonine do in the body?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000282.answer_short: In Wallach's function table, threonine's role is protein production—it's a building block the body uses to manufacture its proteins, alongside valine, lysine, leucine, and isoleucine.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000386.subject: methionine
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000386.question: Why is selenomethionine called the 13th essential amino acid?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000386.answer_short: Selenium researcher Dr. Gerhard Schrauzer called selenomethionine — methionine with a selenium atom in place of its sulfur — the '13th essential amino acid,' Wallach notes.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000387.subject: leucine
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000387.question: Why do people who eat mostly sorghum or millet get pellagra?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000387.answer_short: Wallach notes that in India, where sorghum or millet is a staple, the diet delivers high levels of leucine—and he separately warns that excessive leucine can itself produce pellagra.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000381.subject: tyrosine
WAL-CLM-RARE-000381.question: What does tyrosine have to do with hair and skin color?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000381.answer_short: Tyrosine is the raw material for melanin, the pigment in hair and skin; the enzyme tyrosinase acts on it with copper as a cofactor, so a copper shortage can turn hair white, silver, or gray.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000382.subject: tyrosine
WAL-CLM-RARE-000382.question: Who discovered thyroxin, the thyroid hormone?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000382.answer_short: Wallach recounts that in the first quarter of the 20th century a chemist he names as Kenall isolated a crystalline iodine-tyrosine complex, about 65% iodine, and called it thyroxin -- the thyroid hormone.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000052.subject: methionine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000052.question: What is methionine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000052.answer_short: Methionine is a sulfur-containing essential amino acid; its derivative SAM is the body's main methyl donor, and it's the raw material the body uses to build cysteine, carnitine, taurine, lecithin and phosphatidylcholine.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000053.subject: phenylalanine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000053.question: What does phenylalanine turn into in the body?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000053.answer_short: Phenylalanine is the precursor to tyrosine and, through it, the signaling molecules dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine, plus the pigment melanin (a step that needs copper).

WAL-CLM-LETS-000244.subject: phenylalanine
WAL-CLM-LETS-000244.question: How much phenylalanine does Wallach recommend for depression?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000244.answer_short: For depression, Wallach's protocol includes dl-phenylalanine (with l-tryptophan and l-tyrosine) at 2 grams three times daily, alongside addressing food allergies and hypoglycemia.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000371.subject: phenylalanine
WAL-CLM-LETS-000371.question: How much phenylalanine does Wallach recommend for multiple sclerosis (MS)?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000371.answer_short: For MS, Wallach's protocol includes D-phenylalanine at 500 mg three times a day, alongside removing mercury fillings, fish and flaxseed oil, and other steps.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000462.subject: phenylalanine
WAL-CLM-LETS-000462.question: How much phenylalanine does Wallach recommend for vitiligo?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000462.answer_short: For vitiligo (loss of skin pigment), Wallach's protocol includes phenylalanine at 50 mg per kilogram of body weight per day, with PABA, copper, vitamin A, zinc and B-vitamins.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000159.subject: phenylalanine
WAL-CLM-LETS-000159.question: How much phenylalanine does Wallach recommend for bipolar disorder?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000159.answer_short: For bipolar disorder (manic depression), Wallach's home protocol includes DL-phenylalanine at 5 grams twice daily, alongside chromium/vanadium, essential fatty acids and other steps.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000057.subject: tyrosine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000057.question: What is tyrosine good for?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000057.answer_short: Tyrosine is the precursor for dopamine and norepinephrine, and Wallach reports studies show it helps with stress, fatigue, colds, grief, long work hours, and sleep deprivation, easing stress hormones and boosting mental and physical performance.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000051.subject: lysine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000051.question: How does lysine help build collagen, elastin, and healthy veins?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000051.answer_short: Through its derivative allysine, lysine lets the enzyme lysyl oxidase form the crosslinks that stabilize collagen and elastin, which Wallach says helps prevent and repair spider veins, varicose veins, hemorrhoids, and aneurysms.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000202.subject: lysine
WAL-CLM-LETS-000202.question: How much lysine does Wallach recommend for canker sores?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000202.answer_short: For canker sores, Wallach's protocol includes lysine at 1,500 mg per day, alongside allergen avoidance, zinc, vitamin E, a B-complex, and vitamin A as beta carotene.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000299.subject: lysine
WAL-CLM-LETS-000299.question: How does Wallach treat herpes with lysine?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000299.answer_short: For herpes, Wallach uses L-lysine at 1-6 grams a day to effect, then 500 mg daily for maintenance, plus a high-lysine, low-arginine diet, UV light, vitamin C, bioflavonoids, zinc, and antivirals.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000332.subject: lysine
WAL-CLM-LETS-000332.question: Does Wallach use lysine to treat kidney stones?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000332.answer_short: Yes; lysine (with glutamic acid) is part of Wallach's kidney-stone protocol, alongside calcium and magnesium, reduced phosphorus, vitamin A as beta carotene, vitamin B-6, and specific herbs.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000050.subject: leucine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000050.question: What is leucine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000050.answer_short: Leucine is a branched-chain essential amino acid Wallach says is solely responsible for building muscle protein—a catalyst for muscle growth that also switches on the mTOR kinase controlling cell growth.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000396.subject: leucine
WAL-CLM-LETS-000396.question: How much leucine does Wallach recommend for Parkinson's disease?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000396.answer_short: For drug-induced Parkinsonism, Wallach's protocol includes leucine at 10 grams a day, alongside octacosanol, L-methionine, L-tyrosine, DL-phenylalanine, B-vitamins, essential fatty acids, and digestive enzymes.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000058.subject: valine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000058.question: What is valine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000058.answer_short: Valine is a branched-chain amino acid Wallach counts among the essentials—it supports cognitive function, builds and maintains muscle, and aids exercise recovery and endurance.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000320.subject: valine
WAL-CLM-LETS-000320.question: Can valine help with inflammation?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000320.answer_short: Yes—Wallach's inflammation protocol includes DL-valine at 1.5 grams per day, alongside DMSO, proteolytic enzymes, vitamins C and E, zinc, and other nutrients and herbs.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000048.subject: histidine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000048.question: What is histidine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000048.answer_short: Histidine is an amino acid whose imidazole side chain works in enzyme active sites and binds metals; Wallach also notes it's required for hemoglobin, aiding oxygen binding and resisting carbon monoxide.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000419.subject: histidine
WAL-CLM-LETS-000419.question: How much histidine does Wallach recommend for rheumatoid arthritis?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000419.answer_short: For rheumatoid arthritis, Wallach's protocol includes L-histidine at 1,000 mg three times a day, alongside treatment for Mycoplasma and many other nutrients.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000049.subject: isoleucine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000049.question: How does the body use isoleucine for energy—is it glucogenic or ketogenic?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000049.answer_short: Isoleucine is both glucogenic and ketogenic: part of it can be turned into glucose, while another part is routed into ketone bodies or fatty acids for fuel.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000055.subject: threonine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000055.question: What is threonine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000055.answer_short: Threonine is a polar, protein-building essential amino acid that, with serine, is one of only two amino acids carrying an alcohol group—making it a site for chemical modification and energy production.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000067.subject: omega-9
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000067.question: Is oleic acid a monounsaturated fat, and where is it found?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000067.answer_short: Wallach describes oleic acid as a monounsaturated fat, the same fat found in olive oil, and says it makes up about 30 percent of cocoa butter (the fat in chocolate).

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000068.subject: silica
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000068.question: Does beer contain silica?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000068.answer_short: Wallach notes that beer — often called 'liquid bread' — contains significant levels of silica, the mineral needed for healthy bones, skin, hair and nails.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000069.subject: cesium
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000069.question: Is cesium an essential mineral?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000069.answer_short: Yes, Wallach lists cesium among the essential minerals found in high-quality humic shale, holding that it meets the criteria for an essential nutrient even though it isn't 'classically' considered one.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000070.subject: titanium
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000070.question: Does Wallach say titanium is an essential mineral?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000070.answer_short: Yes — Wallach lists titanium among the essential minerals in humic shale, holding it meets two or more criteria for an essential nutrient.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000071.subject: tantalum
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000071.question: Does Wallach consider tantalum an essential mineral?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000071.answer_short: Yes -- Wallach lists tantalum among the essential minerals found in high-quality humic shale, holding that although such minerals aren't classically considered essential, they each meet two or more criteria for an essential nutrient.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000072.subject: zirconium
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000072.question: Is zirconium an essential nutrient?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000072.answer_short: Wallach argues that although zirconium isn't 'classically' considered essential, it -- like the other plant-derived humic-shale minerals -- meets two or more of the criteria used to declare a nutrient essential.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000394.subject: omega-9
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000394.question: What are the omega-3, omega-6, and omega-9 fatty acid groups?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000394.answer_short: Wallach groups the fatty acids into families -- omega-3 (which he lists as DHA and EPA), omega-6, omega-9, and cholesterol -- though elsewhere he counts only omega-3 and omega-6 as classically essential.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000395.subject: carbon
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000395.question: Why do some minerals have a carbon coating?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000395.answer_short: In Wallach's framework carbon forms a protective coating — a chain of about 10 to 12 carbon atoms — around the third and most stable type of naturally occurring organic mineral colloid.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000396.subject: omega-6
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000396.question: Is arachidonic acid an omega-6 fatty acid?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000396.answer_short: Yes -- Wallach classes arachidonic acid and gamma-linolenic acid as omega-6 fatty acids, both in his 'conditionally essential' group.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000397.subject: omega-6
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000397.question: Were essential fatty acids once called vitamin F?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000397.answer_short: Yes -- Wallach notes the two essential fatty acids were identified in 1923 and first listed as 'vitamin F' before being reclassified as fats.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000398.subject: omega-6
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000398.question: Should omega-3 and omega-6 be balanced?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000398.answer_short: Wallach says yes -- the essential fatty acids' functions in the body all require proper ratios between the omega-3 and omega-6 forms.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000399.subject: omega-6
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000399.question: What does the body make from omega-6 fatty acids?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000399.answer_short: Wallach says omega-6 EFAs are the raw material for lipoxins and other eicosanoid signaling compounds the body produces.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000400.subject: gallium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000400.question: Does gallium act like iron in the body?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000400.answer_short: Wallach says gallium and iron-type (ferric) salts behave so alike in the body that gallium ions often stand in for iron ions in medical treatments.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000401.subject: gallium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000401.question: Is gallium used as a medicine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000401.answer_short: Wallach says gallium maltolate, an orally absorbable form of gallium, is used to treat brain cancer, inflammation, and certain infectious diseases.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000402.subject: gallium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000402.question: Where is gallium found in nature?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000402.answer_short: Wallach says gallium occurs as trace amounts in bauxite and zinc ores and across rocks, water, plants and animals -- richest in shale (about 19 ppm), scarcest in land animals.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000403.subject: aluminum
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000403.question: Is aluminum toxic to humans?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000403.answer_short: Wallach says aluminum is remarkably nontoxic - you'd have to swallow more than a pound of aluminum sulfate in a single day to reach a lethal dose.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000404.subject: aluminum
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000404.question: Is aluminum cookware and deodorant safe?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000404.answer_short: Wallach says studies show aluminum cookware, deodorants, and antiperspirants are generally safe at directed levels, with no evidence they cause disease.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000405.subject: aluminum
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000405.question: Does aluminum affect calcium absorption or bones?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000405.answer_short: Wallach notes aluminum can compete with calcium for absorption, so a high dietary aluminum load can reduce bone mineralization (osteopenia).

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000406.subject: aluminum
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000406.question: Where does the name aluminum come from?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000406.answer_short: The English chemist Sir Humphrey Davy named it aluminum, 'the metal of clay.'

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000407.subject: aluminum
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000407.question: Are rubies and sapphires made of aluminum?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000407.answer_short: Rubies and sapphires are aluminum: Wallach explains aluminum occurs only as the oxide alumina, which becomes those gems when traced with other elements.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000408.subject: gold
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000408.question: Where is gold found in nature?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000408.answer_short: Wallach reports gold occurs only in tiny traces throughout rocks, water, plants and animals -- concentrating in the horsetail plant and forming a colloid in mammalian livers.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000409.subject: gold
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000409.question: Did alchemists try to turn lead into gold?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000409.answer_short: Wallach says medieval alchemists -- the earliest chemists -- spent most of their effort trying to transmute lead and other base metals into gold, which was seen as a noble cure-all.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000410.subject: gold
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000410.question: Did the ancient Chinese believe gold could make you immortal?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000410.answer_short: Wallach says the Chinese believed gold was immortal and could confer immortality -- even holding that eating daily from gold-colored alloy plates was enough.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000411.subject: gold
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000411.question: What are the side effects of gold treatment for arthritis?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000411.answer_short: Wallach lists gold-therapy toxic reactions including itching, dermatitis, mouth inflammation, GI upset, protein or blood in the urine, aplastic anemia, low white cells, hepatitis and pneumonitis.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000412.subject: bromine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000412.question: Who discovered bromine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000412.answer_short: Wallach recounts that bromine was discovered independently by two chemists — Carl Jacob Lowig in 1825 and Antoine Balard in 1826.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000413.subject: bromine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000413.question: Is bromine toxic?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000413.answer_short: Wallach warns that toxic reactions from a bromine overdose can resemble acne-like skin eruptions.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000414.subject: lanthanum
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000414.question: What is lanthanum?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000414.answer_short: Lanthanum (symbol La) is what Wallach calls a 'light' rare earth metal, one of the rare earths he counts among the body's essential minerals.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000415.subject: lanthanum
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000415.question: Is lanthanum found in the human body?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000415.answer_short: Yes; Wallach reports lanthanum occurs in animal tissue at trace levels and concentrates in bone (about 0.27 ppm) far more than in soft tissue (0.0001 ppm).

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000416.subject: cerium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000416.question: What is cerium?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000416.answer_short: Cerium is a Rare Earth element — the most abundant of all the rare earths — named after Ceres, the Roman goddess of agriculture.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000417.subject: cerium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000417.question: Who discovered cerium and when?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000417.answer_short: Cerium was discovered in 1803 at Bastnas, Sweden by Berzelius and Hisinger, and in Germany by Martin Heinrich Klaproth.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000418.subject: cerium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000418.question: What plants is cerium found in?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000418.answer_short: Wallach says cerium is commonly found in tobacco plants, barley, and the wood of beech trees.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000419.subject: beryllium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000419.question: What is beryllium?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000419.answer_short: Beryllium is a rare, light, hard gray-white alkaline-earth metal that Wallach lists among the body's essential minerals and that occurs mainly locked inside gemstones like beryl and emerald.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000420.subject: beryllium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000420.question: Who discovered beryllium?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000420.answer_short: Beryllium was discovered in 1798 by French chemist Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin, who isolated it as a new 'rare earth' from emerald and beryl.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000421.subject: beryllium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000421.question: Where does the name beryllium come from?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000421.answer_short: Beryllium was first called 'glucine' or 'glucinium' for its sweet taste, and only got the name 'beryllium,' coined by Wohler in 1828, much later.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000422.subject: rubidium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000422.question: What is rubidium?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000422.answer_short: Rubidium is a plant-derived trace mineral that Wallach counts among the 60 essential elements the body needs.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000423.subject: rubidium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000423.question: Where is rubidium found in the body?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000423.answer_short: Wallach reports rubidium's highest levels in land animals concentrate in the liver and muscle, with the lowest levels in bone.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000424.subject: erbium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000424.question: Is erbium found in the body?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000424.answer_short: Yes — Wallach reports that in land animals erbium settles primarily in bone, while plants take it up strongly, reaching up to 46 ppm in Carya species.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000425.subject: europium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000425.question: Where is europium found in nature and in the body?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000425.answer_short: Europium is a plant-derived rare-earth trace mineral that spreads thinly through rocks, plants and animals -- and in land animals it concentrates in bone far more than in soft tissue.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000426.subject: europium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000426.question: Who discovered europium and how?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000426.answer_short: William Crookes observed the phosphorescent spectra of the rare earths in the late 1880s, but europium's discovery is generally credited to French chemist Eugene-Anatole Demarcay, who isolated it in 1901.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000427.subject: cesium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000427.question: Is cesium found in the body?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000427.answer_short: Yes, Wallach reports cesium occurs in trace amounts in plants and animals, and in land animals the highest concentrations are found in the muscle.
topics: is cesium found in the body

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000428.subject: barium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000428.question: Where does the name barium come from?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000428.answer_short: Barium's name traces to the alchemical term 'baryta,' from the Greek 'barys,' meaning 'heavy.'

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000429.subject: barium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000429.question: When was barium discovered?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000429.answer_short: Wallach says barium was isolated as an element in 1774 but not classed as a metal until 1808, the year he credits to English chemist Sir Humphry Davy.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000430.subject: barium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000430.question: Which plants are highest in barium?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000430.answer_short: Wallach reports barium is highest in marine plants like brown algae, and the fruit of Bertholletia excelea is such a strong barium concentrator it can hold up to 4,000 ppm.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000431.subject: yttrium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000431.question: Is yttrium found in the human body?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000431.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says yttrium turns up in living tissue, accumulating in ferns among plants and settling into mammalian bone, teeth and liver.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000432.subject: arsenic
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000432.question: Where does the word arsenic come from?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000432.answer_short: Wallach traces 'arsenic' from the Syriac al zarniga and Persian Zarnikh ('yellow pigment') through Greek arsenikos (meaning 'masculine'), then Latin arsenicum and Old French arsenic.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000433.subject: arsenic
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000433.question: Who discovered arsenic and when?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000433.answer_short: Wallach records that arsenic was first isolated and identified in 1250 by Albertus Magnus.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000434.subject: arsenic
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000434.question: What has arsenic been used to treat?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000434.answer_short: Wallach says arsenic compounds have long served as medicines — arsphenamine and neosalvarsan for syphilis and trypanosomiasis, and arsenic trioxide for cancer and, from 2000, leukemia.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000435.subject: tin
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000435.question: What is tin?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000435.answer_short: Tin (symbol Sn) is a trace mineral Wallach counts among the essential elements; chemically it sits in the fourth main group, resembling carbon, silica, germanium, and lead.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000436.subject: tin
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000436.question: Is tin found in the human body?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000436.answer_short: Yes -- Wallach says tin occurs in land animals with the highest levels in the lungs and intestines of vertebrates, and in plants it concentrates most in mosses (bryophytes) and lichens.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000437.subject: tin
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000437.question: Why do men lose their hearing faster than women?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000437.answer_short: Wallach points to a 1991 federal study finding men now have poorer hearing at any age, thought to result from tin deficiency, with men over 30 losing hearing more than twice as fast as women.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000438.subject: praseodymium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000438.question: Is praseodymium found in the body?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000438.answer_short: Wallach says praseodymium accumulates in mammalian bone and liver, and land plants concentrate it up to 46 ppm.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000439.subject: rhenium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000439.question: Does Wallach say rhenium is essential?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000439.answer_short: Yes — Wallach lists rhenium among the 60 essential elements, metals, minerals, trace minerals and rare earths he holds the body requires.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000440.subject: thulium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000440.question: Is thulium found in plants and animals?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000440.answer_short: Wallach reports that thulium occurs naturally in land plants and land animals, but only in extraordinarily tiny trace amounts.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000441.subject: samarium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000441.question: What is samarium?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000441.answer_short: Samarium is a 'light' rare earth element that Wallach counts among the trace minerals the body needs.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000442.subject: samarium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000442.question: Is samarium found in the human body?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000442.answer_short: Wallach says samarium is present in living tissue in tiny amounts, in heart muscle, bone and liver, and that plants accumulate it.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000443.subject: ytterbium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000443.question: What is ytterbium?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000443.answer_short: Ytterbium (Yb) is a rare-earth trace element Wallach documents in rocks, soil, plants and animals -- and it concentrates in bone, teeth and liver.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000283.subject: carbon
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000283.question: Are minerals carbon-based?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000283.answer_short: No — Wallach teaches that minerals are the body's non-carbon raw materials that come from the soil, while the carbon-based nutrients (carbohydrates, fats, proteins and vitamins) are built using the sun's energy.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000284.subject: oxygen
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000284.question: What is oxygen and why does the body need it?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000284.answer_short: Oxygen is one of the three obvious raw materials every living thing needs to sustain life, and unlike food it is a 'non-variable' — the same everywhere on earth.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000285.subject: strontium
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000285.question: Does the body need strontium?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000285.answer_short: Wallach holds there is considerable evidence that strontium is an essential mineral in mammals, including humans.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000286.subject: strontium
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000286.question: What is strontium-90, and is it natural?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000286.answer_short: Strontium-90 is a man-made radioactive product of atomic-bomb fission — the great biohazard scare of the Cold War — and, unlike natural strontium, it does not occur in nature.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000287.subject: tin
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000287.question: Does tin help regrow hair?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000287.answer_short: Wallach says tin deficiency causes male-pattern baldness in lab animals, and he personally regrew a considerable amount of hair using plant-derived liquid colloidal tin.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000388.subject: gallium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000388.question: Where does the name gallium come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000388.answer_short: Gallium was named for Gallia, the Latin word for France, and was identified in 1875 by the chemist Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000389.subject: gallium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000389.question: Can taking gallium during pregnancy lower a child's risk of brain cancer?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000389.answer_short: Wallach cites British research finding that pregnant women whose diets are supplemented with gallium have significantly lower rates of brain cancer in their children.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000390.subject: hydrogen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000390.question: Where does the name hydrogen come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000390.answer_short: Hydrogen means 'water-creator' in Greek, because burning it in oxygen produces water.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000391.subject: hydrogen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000391.question: Is hydrogen gas flammable?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000391.answer_short: Yes, Wallach describes hydrogen as a colorless, odorless, tasteless but extremely flammable diatomic gas.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000392.subject: hydrogen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000392.question: Where is hydrogen found in nature?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000392.answer_short: Wallach reports hydrogen is most concentrated in water, about 111,000 ppm in fresh water and 108,000 ppm in seawater, with smaller amounts in rocks and living tissue.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000393.subject: nitrogen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000393.question: Are the nitrates and nitrites in processed meat bad for you?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000393.answer_short: Wallach warns that nitrates and nitrites in cured and canned foods turn into nitrosamines in the stomach -- potential carcinogens that can also suppress the thyroid.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000394.subject: oxygen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000394.question: Why do I need minerals to use oxygen?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000394.answer_short: Wallach says even oxygen and water are useless to your cells without mineral cofactors — no nutrient works physiologically without minerals.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000395.subject: oxygen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000395.question: Is oxygen poisonous?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000395.answer_short: Wallach approvingly cites Dr. Roy Walford's point that the oxygen in our atmosphere is actually a highly poisonous gas — one we both require and are damaged by.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000396.subject: oxygen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000396.question: Do cancer cells die in the presence of oxygen?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000396.answer_short: Wallach cites Otto Warburg's Nobel-winning finding that cancer cells ferment sugar anaerobically and die in the presence of oxygen, while normal cells run on aerobic metabolism.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000397.subject: oxygen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000397.question: What is hyperbaric oxygen therapy used for?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000397.answer_short: Wallach says exposing patients to several atmospheres of oxygen in a hyperbaric chamber can reactivate 'sleeping beauty' cells around a stroke and speed the healing of athletic injuries.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000398.subject: oxygen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000398.question: How long has oxygen therapy been used in medicine?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000398.answer_short: Wallach says oxygen in the form of hydrogen peroxide has been used topically, intravenously, and orally since the Civil War, and widely in Europe for over 50 years.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000399.subject: silica
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000399.question: What is silica?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000399.answer_short: Silica is silicon dioxide (SiO2), the most important compound of silicon — the second most abundant element in the earth's crust after oxygen — and Wallach counts it among the body's essential minerals.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000400.subject: silica
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000400.question: Is silica the same as sand and glass?
