WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000400.answer_short: Wallach explains that silica is the main material of sand, and that sand melted with soda ash and limestone becomes glass — of which there are more than a thousand forms.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000401.subject: aluminum
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000401.question: Is there aluminum in baby formula?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000401.answer_short: Wallach cites a survey putting aluminum in infant formula at about 0.9 mg/kg body weight per week (milk-based) and 1.1 mg (soy-based).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000402.subject: gold
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000402.question: What is gold?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000402.answer_short: Wallach describes gold as the most precious and one of the most beautiful of all metals -- a corrosion-resistant, bright-yellow element prized since ancient times.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000403.subject: gold
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000403.question: Where does the name gold and its symbol Au come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000403.answer_short: Wallach says gold's symbol Au comes from the Latin aurum ('shining dawn'), with older roots in the Sanskrit jval and the Anglo-Saxon gold.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000404.subject: gold
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000404.question: Is gold used in dental fillings?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000404.answer_short: Wallach notes gold dissolves in mercury to form an amalgam, and this gold-mercury amalgam is used by dentists to fill teeth.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000405.subject: strontium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000405.question: Where does the name strontium come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000405.answer_short: Strontium was named in 1789 after the Scottish village of Strontian, where Dr. Adair Crawford first identified the element.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000406.subject: bromine
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000406.question: Is bromine a liquid?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000406.answer_short: In its pure form bromine is a reddish liquid, and Wallach notes it and mercury are the only two elements that are liquid at room temperature.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000407.subject: bromine
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000407.question: What does the name bromine mean?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000407.answer_short: Wallach explains the element was named bromine from the Greek word 'bromos,' which means 'stench.'

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000408.subject: terbium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000408.question: What is terbium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000408.answer_short: Terbium is a rare-earth metal that Wallach counts among the essential trace minerals -- one of the least abundant of the rare earths, silvery-white and soft enough to be cut with a knife.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000409.subject: terbium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000409.question: Who discovered terbium and when?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000409.answer_short: Wallach records that terbium was discovered in 1843 by Carl Gustaf Mosander, who isolated its oxide from the mineral yttria.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000410.subject: terbium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000410.question: Where does terbium come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000410.answer_short: Wallach says terbium is recovered commercially from monazite -- a mix of rare earths, thorium and calcium -- found in river sands from India and Brazil and beach sand from Florida.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000411.subject: rubidium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000411.question: Who discovered rubidium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000411.answer_short: Rubidium was discovered in 1861 by German chemists Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff, who spotted it by its deep-red spectral line.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000412.subject: rubidium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000412.question: Where does the name rubidium come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000412.answer_short: The name rubidium comes from the Latin rubidus, meaning 'deep red,' after the red spectral line by which it was identified.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000413.subject: nickel
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000413.question: What is nickel?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000413.answer_short: Wallach describes nickel as a silvery metal and a rare element, making up only one one-hundredth of one percent of the earth's crust.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000414.subject: nickel
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000414.question: Where does the name nickel come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000414.answer_short: Wallach says nickel is a German word for Satan, from Kupfernickel, meaning 'Satan's copper.'

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000415.subject: nickel
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000415.question: Who discovered nickel?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000415.answer_short: Wallach says nickel's pure metal was first identified in 1751 by Swedish chemist Axel Fredrik Cronstedt.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000416.subject: nickel
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000416.question: What is nickel used for?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000416.answer_short: Wallach says nickel is used in the US five-cent coin, in powerful alnico magnets, and in nickel-cadmium (Ni-Cad) batteries.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000417.subject: barium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000417.question: Is barium a rare element?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000417.answer_short: No — despite being grouped with the rare earths, Wallach calls barium an abundant element, ranking sixth among all the elements in the earth's crust.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000418.subject: neodymium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000418.question: Who discovered neodymium and when?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000418.answer_short: Wallach's book recounts that neodymium was discovered in 1885 by Austrian amateur mineralogist Baron Carl Auer von Welsbach, who split the mineral didymium into two new elements.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000419.subject: neodymium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000419.question: Where does the name neodymium come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000419.answer_short: Welsbach coined 'neodymium' from two Greek words, neos ('new') and didymos ('twin'), after splitting the mineral didymium.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000420.subject: neodymium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000420.question: What is neodymium used for?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000420.answer_short: Wallach's book notes neodymium is used to make the most powerful magnets on earth, plus colored glass for welder's goggles and the synthetic 'ruby' in powerful lasers.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000421.subject: yttrium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000421.question: What is yttrium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000421.answer_short: Yttrium is a 'heavy' rare earth element — a silver-gray metal Wallach counts among the plant-derived trace minerals the body needs.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000422.subject: yttrium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000422.question: Where does the name yttrium come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000422.answer_short: Yttrium was first identified in 1789 by Johan Gadolin, who named it for Ytterby, a small Swedish village near Stockholm.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000423.subject: yttrium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000423.question: Did the Apollo astronauts find yttrium on the moon?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000423.answer_short: Wallach says yttrium is scarce in the earth's crust, but moon rocks the Apollo astronauts brought back had a surprisingly high level of it.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000424.subject: arsenic
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000424.question: What is arsenic?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000424.answer_short: Arsenic is a semimetal or metalloid that occurs mostly in mineral compounds such as realgar and orpiment, both of which are mixes of arsenic and sulfur.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000425.subject: lutetium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000425.question: Where does the name lutetium come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000425.answer_short: The name comes from Lutetia, the ancient name for the city of Paris, coined by the French scientist Georges Urbain.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000426.subject: lutetium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000426.question: Who discovered lutetium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000426.answer_short: Lutetium was discovered in 1907 by the Austrian mineralogist Carl Auer von Welsbach and the French scientist Georges Urbain, with American chemist Charles James believed to have found it independently the same year.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000427.subject: niobium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000427.question: What is niobium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000427.answer_short: Wallach describes niobium as a soft, steel-gray metal found mainly in the ore columbite.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000428.subject: niobium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000428.question: Who discovered niobium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000428.answer_short: Wallach says niobium was discovered by the Englishman Charles Hatchett in 1801.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000429.subject: niobium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000429.question: Where does the name niobium come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000429.answer_short: Wallach says the element was named niobium for the mythological goddess Niobe.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000430.subject: praseodymium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000430.question: What is praseodymium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000430.answer_short: Praseodymium is a soft, silvery-white 'light' rare earth metal that tarnishes to a green oxide, one of the rare-earth minerals Wallach counts among the essential nutrients.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000431.subject: praseodymium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000431.question: Who discovered praseodymium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000431.answer_short: Praseodymium was isolated in 1885 by the Austrian baron Carl Auer von Welsbach, who split the mineral didymium into two new elements.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000432.subject: praseodymium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000432.question: Where does the name praseodymium come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000432.answer_short: The name comes from the Greek 'prasios' (green) and 'didymos' (twin), for the green color of the element's oxide.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000433.subject: titanium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000433.question: What is titanium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000433.answer_short: Titanium is the ninth most abundant element in the earth's crust — a trace mineral discovered in 1791 and named for the Titans of Greek myth.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000434.subject: titanium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000434.question: Where does the name titanium come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000434.answer_short: Titanium is named for the Titans of Greek mythology.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000435.subject: titanium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000435.question: What is titanium used for?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000435.answer_short: Wallach points to titanium's industrial scale — each Boeing 747 jet engine holds 10,000 pounds of it.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000436.subject: scandium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000436.question: What is scandium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000436.answer_short: Scandium is a rare element that makes up only about 0.0025% of the earth's crust and occurs at an even higher rate in the sun and a few other stars.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000437.subject: scandium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000437.question: Who discovered scandium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000437.answer_short: Scandium was predicted by Mendeleyev in 1871 from the periodic chart and then discovered in 1879 by Lars Fredrik Nilson.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000438.subject: scandium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000438.question: Where does the name scandium come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000438.answer_short: When Lars Fredrik Nilson discovered scandium in 1879 he named it after his homeland, Scandinavia.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000439.subject: rhenium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000439.question: What is rhenium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000439.answer_short: Rhenium is one of the rarest elements on Earth — so scarce that a million pounds of ore yields only a single gram.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000440.subject: rhenium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000440.question: Who discovered rhenium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000440.answer_short: Rhenium's existence was predicted and then discovered in 1925 by German chemists Ida Tacke, Walter Nodack, and Otto Carl Berg.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000441.subject: rhenium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000441.question: Where does the name rhenium come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000441.answer_short: Rhenium is named from the Latin word Rhenus, which translates to the Rhine River.
topics: where does the name come from

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000442.subject: dysprosium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000442.question: What is dysprosium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000442.answer_short: Dysprosium is a soft, shiny, silvery rare-earth metal — soft enough to be cut with a knife and fairly stable in air.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000443.subject: dysprosium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000443.question: What is dysprosium used for?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000443.answer_short: Wallach notes dysprosium forms alloys whose magnetic features help compact discs function efficiently.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000444.subject: thulium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000444.question: What is thulium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000444.answer_short: Thulium is a soft, bright silvery 'heavy' rare-earth metal, so soft it can be cut with a knife, and one of the scarcest of the rare earths.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000445.subject: thulium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000445.question: Who discovered thulium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000445.answer_short: Thulium was discovered in 1879 by the Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve, who isolated its greenish oxide from the mineral erbia.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000446.subject: thulium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000446.question: Where does the name thulium come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000446.answer_short: Thulium is named after Thule, the ancient name for Scandinavia, chosen by its discoverer Per Teodor Cleve.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000447.subject: thulium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000447.question: Where does thulium come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000447.answer_short: Wallach says thulium's main source is the mineral monazite, found in river sands in India and Brazil and in beach sand in Florida.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000448.subject: samarium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000448.question: Who discovered samarium and when?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000448.answer_short: Samarium was discovered in 1879 by the French chemist Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000449.subject: samarium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000449.question: Where does the name samarium come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000449.answer_short: Wallach says samarium was identified in a mineral called samarskite, which was itself named for a Russian army officer, Colonel Samarski.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000450.subject: ytterbium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000450.question: Where does the name ytterbium come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000450.answer_short: Wallach says ytterbium was discovered in 1878 by French chemist Jean de Marignac and named after the small Swedish village of Ytterby.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000451.subject: holmium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000451.question: Who discovered holmium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000451.answer_short: Two Swiss chemists first spotted holmium's spectral lines in 1878 but couldn't identify it, and Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve isolated and named it in 1879.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000452.subject: holmium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000452.question: Where does the name holmium come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000452.answer_short: Holmium is named Holmia -- Latin for Stockholm, the home town of Per Teodor Cleve, the Swedish chemist who isolated it in 1879.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000453.subject: tantalum
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000453.question: Where does the name tantalum come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000453.answer_short: Wallach recounts that the Swedish chemist Anders Gustav Ekeberg, who discovered the element in 1802, named it after Tantalos, the father of Niobe in Greek mythology.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000454.subject: tantalum
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000454.question: Was tantalum confused with niobium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000454.answer_short: For nearly 50 years after Ekeberg announced it, many chemists thought he had mistaken tantalum for niobium, and pure tantalum metal was not produced until 1903.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000455.subject: tantalum
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000455.question: What is tantalum used for?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000455.answer_short: Wallach notes that tantalum -- whose principal ore is columbite -- is used for dental and joint prosthesis.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000456.subject: hafnium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000456.question: What is hafnium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000456.answer_short: Hafnium is a bright, silvery-white metal so chemically bound to its 'twin' zirconium that the two are almost impossible to separate, and Wallach counts it among his essential trace minerals.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000457.subject: hafnium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000457.question: Where does the name hafnium come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000457.answer_short: Hafnium is named for Copenhagen; its finders Coster and von Hevesy honored Bohr's native city using its Latin name, Hafnia.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000458.subject: zirconium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000458.question: What is zirconium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000458.answer_short: Zirconium is a mineral Wallach counts among the essential trace elements and rare earths; its best-known form is the gemstone mineral zircon, a crystalline zirconium silicate.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000459.subject: zirconium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000459.question: Who discovered zirconium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000459.answer_short: Zirconium was discovered in 1787 by the German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth, though its best-known compound, zircon, had been known since ancient times.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000460.subject: zirconium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000460.question: Where does the name zirconium come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000460.answer_short: The name zirconium comes from 'zargun,' the Arabic word for zircon, which translates to 'gold color.'

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000461.subject: zirconium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000461.question: Is zirconium related to hafnium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000461.answer_short: Yes -- zirconium and hafnium are chemical twins, so alike that Wallach says it is almost impossible to work with one without working with the other.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000462.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000462.question: Is there real proof that rare-earth minerals extend life?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000462.answer_short: Yes — Wallach cites lab studies where adding rare-earth minerals to animals' diets doubled their expected lifespan, and argues that because these minerals are stripped from our food, daily supplementation is the only reliable way to get them.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000383.subject: hydrogen
WAL-CLM-RARE-000383.question: How does the body use hydrogen peroxide to fight infection?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000383.answer_short: Wallach says neutrophils (white blood cells) make hydrogen peroxide as a 'lethal weapon' to destroy germs and cancer cells, while the enzyme catalase protects healthy tissue from the excess.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000384.subject: nitrogen
WAL-CLM-RARE-000384.question: Where is nitrogen found and how much is in the body?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000384.answer_short: Wallach reports nitrogen rising from about 20 ppm in igneous rock to 100,000 ppm in land animals, showing it concentrates strongly in living tissue.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000385.subject: silica
WAL-CLM-RARE-000385.question: What parts of the body contain silica?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000385.answer_short: Wallach says silica is present in the blood, bile, skin, hair and nails, and forms part of the connective tissue, bones, nerve sheaths and mucus membranes.
topics: where is silica in the body

WAL-CLM-RARE-000386.subject: silver
WAL-CLM-RARE-000386.question: Why are newborn babies given silver drops in their eyes?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000386.answer_short: Wallach recounts that in 1884 Carl Sigmund Crede began the practice of putting a single prophylactic drop of 2% silver nitrate in every newborn's eyes to prevent gonorrheal eye infection at birth.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000387.subject: silver
WAL-CLM-RARE-000387.question: Why is silver linked to the moon and lunacy?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000387.answer_short: In Wallach's history of medicine, silver was tied to the moon -- believed to rule the head and emotions -- so 'Tincture of the moon' (a silver preparation) was long used for epilepsy, melancholia, and mania.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000388.subject: silver
WAL-CLM-RARE-000388.question: What conditions can colloidal silver help with?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000388.answer_short: Wallach cites a 1917 British Medical Journal report by J. Mark Hovell that colloidal silver helped ear, nose and throat problems -- blocked eustachian tubes, nasal catarrh, mouth/throat/ear infections -- plus septicemia, cystitis, whooping cough and shingles.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000389.subject: silver
WAL-CLM-RARE-000389.question: Does colloidal silver survive stomach acid when you swallow it?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000389.answer_short: Wallach says that taken internally, colloidal silver particles resist the dilute acids and alkalis of the stomach and intestine, so they keep their catalytic action and pass into the intestine unchanged.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000390.subject: silver
WAL-CLM-RARE-000390.question: Has silver been used to treat cancer?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000390.answer_short: Wallach reports that Dr. Bjorn Nordstrom of Sweden's Karolinska Institute has used silver in his alternative cancer therapy programs.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000391.subject: aluminum
WAL-CLM-RARE-000391.question: Was aluminum ever more valuable than silver?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000391.answer_short: Yes - Wallach recounts that aluminum was once worth more than silver, until Charles Hall's 1886 electrolysis process made it cheap.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000392.subject: gold
WAL-CLM-RARE-000392.question: Was gold one of the first metals humans discovered?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000392.answer_short: Wallach holds that gold, silver and copper were probably the first metals discovered in their native nugget form -- with gold likely the very first.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000393.subject: cerium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000393.question: Was cerium ever used as a medicine?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000393.answer_short: Yes — in the 1800s physicians used cerium salts to control morning sickness and severe vomiting.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000394.subject: nickel
WAL-CLM-RARE-000394.question: Was nickel ever used as a medicine?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000394.answer_short: Wallach recounts that bromide of nickel was used in the 1800s as a therapy for epilepsy and similar diseases.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000395.subject: barium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000395.question: Was barium ever used as a medicine?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000395.answer_short: Yes — Wallach recounts that 18th-century physician Adair Crawford used chlorinated barium to treat 'scrophulous' (TB of the cervical lymph nodes), believing it improved appetite and general health, though it could cause nausea and vertigo.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000396.subject: arsenic
WAL-CLM-RARE-000396.question: Isn't arsenic a poison — why would I need it?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000396.answer_short: Wallach holds that although arsenic is feared as a poison, in trace levels it is in fact an essential element for optimal health and longevity.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000397.subject: tin
WAL-CLM-RARE-000397.question: How was tin used in medicine historically?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000397.answer_short: Wallach recounts that in the Middle Ages Paracelsus recommended tin to expel worms, and tin was also used as a sweat-inducer and a purgative for fevers, PMS, and venereal disease.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000517.subject: nitrogen
WAL-CLM-LETS-000517.question: What is BUN (blood urea nitrogen) and what does it mean?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000517.answer_short: BUN, or blood urea nitrogen, is a barometer of how well the liver and kidneys process the by-products of protein metabolism.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000049.subject: carbon
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000049.question: What is carbon?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000049.answer_short: Wallach calls carbon the element most essential for life on Earth — the structural backbone of every organic molecule, from carbohydrates, fats and amino acids to vitamins and enzymes.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000084.subject: gallium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000084.question: Is gallium an essential mineral?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000084.answer_short: Wallach counts gallium among the essential elements, noting it was claimed essential in 1938 and again in 1958 and has metalloenzyme activity in the human brain.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000135.subject: gallium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000135.question: Does gallium help protect against brain cancer?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000135.answer_short: Wallach says gallium has specific metalloenzyme activity in the human brain and has been reported to specifically reduce the rate of brain cancer in laboratory animals.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000153.subject: hydrogen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000153.question: Does cranberry juice help bladder infections?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000153.answer_short: Wallach says acidifying the urine with unsweetened cranberry juice can often control bladder infections (cystitis).

WAL-CLM-RARE-000182.subject: nitrogen
WAL-CLM-RARE-000182.question: What is nitrogen and what does it do in the body?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000182.answer_short: Nitrogen is a structural atom in protein, in the nucleic acids RNA and DNA, and in many organic molecules, supplied to the body as dietary protein.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000185.subject: nitrogen
WAL-CLM-RARE-000185.question: What happens if you don't get enough protein?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000185.answer_short: Classic protein deficiency causes infertility, poor growth, lowered immune status, edema, and Kwashiorkor -- the potbellied, thin children of third-world countries.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000183.subject: nitrogen
WAL-CLM-RARE-000183.question: What does the body use protein for?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000183.answer_short: Protein's core uses are repairing worn-out tissue, building new tissue (muscle, growth, pregnancy), and serving as an emergency source of heat and energy.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000244.subject: silica
WAL-CLM-RARE-000244.question: Does silica help build collagen and strengthen bones?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000244.answer_short: Wallach says silicon (silica) supplementation increases the collagen in growing bone by 100%, and that tissue silicon levels fall with age in people who don't supplement.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000245.subject: silica
WAL-CLM-RARE-000245.question: What are the signs of silica deficiency?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000245.answer_short: Wallach says silica deficiency shows up as dry brittle hair, brittle finger and toe nails, poor skin quality, poor calcium utilization, and arterial disease.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000246.subject: silica
WAL-CLM-RARE-000246.question: How much silica should you take a day?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000246.answer_short: Wallach gives a recommended silicon (silica) intake of 200 to 500 mg per day, and notes high-fiber diets are rich in silicon, which many investigators think helps lower cholesterol.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000027.subject: silver
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000027.question: What is silver?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000027.answer_short: Silver is a mineral Wallach counts as essential -- not because an enzyme requires it, but because it works as a systemic disinfectant and immune-system stimulator, so a silver deficiency leaves the immune system impaired.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000030.subject: silver
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000030.question: Can taking too much silver turn your skin blue-gray?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000030.answer_short: Wallach says silver is absolutely non-toxic at standard intake, but chronic overdosing can cause argyria -- a permanent, whole-body dusky blue-gray discoloration of the skin.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000028.subject: silver
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000028.question: How does silver kill bacteria and viruses?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000028.answer_short: Per Wallach, silver is an anti-bacterial, anti-viral, anti-fungal 'anti-metabolite' that disables the specific enzymes microorganisms use to breathe (respire) -- so efficient that our great-grandmothers dropped silver dollars into milk to keep it from spoiling.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000090.subject: silver
WAL-CLM-RARE-000090.question: How much silver can you take per day?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000090.answer_short: Wallach says humans can consume 400 mcg of silver per day, and that a silver 'deficiency' results in an impaired immune system.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000032.subject: aluminum
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000032.question: Is aluminum an essential nutrient?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000032.answer_short: Yes - Wallach classifies the organically-bound colloidal aluminum in soil-grown plants as an essential, nontoxic nutrient, and lab-diet aluminum deficiency caused congenital limb defects.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000067.subject: gold
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000067.question: Is the gold leaf in fancy foods and drinks good for you?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000067.answer_short: Wallach says elemental gold leaf is biologically inert -- tasteless, unabsorbed and passed unchanged in the feces -- so the gold in gourmet foods and $1,000 cocktails is purely decorative with no nutritional value.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000096.subject: gold
WAL-CLM-RARE-000096.question: Does gold treat arthritis and how is it given?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000096.answer_short: Wallach documents that gold compounds are injected as an add-on to aspirin for arthritis -- not as a painkiller but for anti-inflammatory effect -- starting around 10 mg weekly and building toward a one-gram total.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000097.subject: gold
WAL-CLM-RARE-000097.question: Who should not take gold compounds?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000097.answer_short: Wallach warns gold compounds must not be used in patients with liver or kidney disease, blood diseases, or systemic lupus erythematosus (lupus).

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000033.subject: strontium
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000033.question: What is strontium?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000033.answer_short: Strontium is a trace mineral that can substitute for calcium in the body and is most highly concentrated in bone.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000032.subject: strontium
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000032.question: Can a strontium deficiency cause osteoporosis?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000032.answer_short: Wallach links strontium deficiency to certain calcium- and boron-resistant forms of osteoporosis and arthritis.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000250.subject: strontium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000250.question: Is strontium radioactive or dangerous?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000250.answer_short: Natural strontium is a needed mineral; strontium-90 is a separate man-made radioactive fission product that does not occur in nature.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000047.subject: bromine
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000047.question: What is bromine?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000047.answer_short: Bromine is a halogen in the same chemical family as iodine that Wallach counts among the essential minerals, working in the body in its active form as brominated amino acids.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000103.subject: bromine
WAL-CLM-RARE-000103.question: How does bromine work in the body?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000103.answer_short: Wallach says bromine functions in the body through brominated amino acids, and holds there is strong evidence it is essential for mammals.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000095.subject: lanthanum
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000095.question: Can candida cause chronic fatigue?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000095.answer_short: Wallach theorizes that Candida albicans produces an energy-sapping, chronic-fatigue-like illness by hoarding lanthanum and 'stealing' it from the patient.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000158.subject: lanthanum
WAL-CLM-RARE-000158.question: Can lanthanum extend lifespan?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000158.answer_short: Wallach reports that a trace of lanthanum (0.32 ppm) doubles the life span of the protozoa Blepharisma and Tetrahymena pyriformis and speeds their growth.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000075.subject: cerium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000075.question: Does cerium act like calcium in the body?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000075.answer_short: Wallach says cerium can function much like calcium in all organisms — it deposits in bone and has been shown to stimulate metabolism.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000070.subject: beryllium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000070.question: Is beryllium toxic?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000070.answer_short: Yes - Wallach warns that pure powdered beryllium and its compounds must be handled carefully because they can cause acute beryllium disease or chemical pneumonitis.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000045.subject: beryllium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000045.question: What is berylliosis?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000045.answer_short: Berylliosis is a painful, sometimes fatal lung disease Wallach says comes from inhaling beryllium oxide dust from mining and industry.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000287.subject: beryllium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000287.question: Where is beryllium found in nature?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000287.answer_short: Wallach records beryllium as a rare element present only in trace amounts across igneous rocks, shale, sandstone, soil, and fresh and sea water.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000298.subject: terbium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000298.question: Does terbium build up in the body?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000298.answer_short: In Wallach's periodic-table survey, terbium occurs only in trace amounts across rocks, plants, and animals, and in land animals it accumulates in mammalian bone.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000217.subject: rubidium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000217.question: Can rubidium replace potassium in the body?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000217.answer_short: Wallach notes rubidium can take over potassium's electrolyte function in many species — including bacteria, algae, fungi, and invertebrates such as starfish.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000105.subject: nickel
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000105.question: Is nickel an essential mineral?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000105.answer_short: Yes — Wallach holds that nickel is an essential trace mineral that acts as a cofactor for metalloenzymes and helps the gut absorb iron and zinc.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000192.subject: nickel
WAL-CLM-RARE-000192.question: Where is nickel found in the body?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000192.answer_short: Wallach reports nickel accumulates in RNA, and that less than 10 percent of ingested metallic nickel is actually absorbed.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000193.subject: nickel
WAL-CLM-RARE-000193.question: What are the symptoms of nickel deficiency?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000193.answer_short: Wallach lists poor growth, anemia, depressed liver oxidative ability, high newborn mortality, a rough/dry coat, dermatitis, delayed puberty, and poor zinc absorption.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000194.subject: nickel
WAL-CLM-RARE-000194.question: Does nickel interact with vitamin B12?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000194.answer_short: Wallach says nickel and vitamin B12 are interdependent — B12 is needed for nickel to work, and B12 deficiency raises the body's need for nickel.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000080.subject: erbium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000080.question: Where does the name erbium come from?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000080.answer_short: Erbium is named for Ytterby, a village in Sweden, from the yttria that Carl Gustaf Mosander split into three fractions in 1843.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000081.subject: europium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000081.question: Can europium help you live longer?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000081.answer_short: Wallach reports that europium doubled the lifespan of a laboratory species (the protozoan Tetrahymena pyriformis) -- a 100 percent increase over its normal expected lifespan.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000115.subject: europium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000115.question: Is europium found in breast milk?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000115.answer_short: Yes -- Wallach reports europium occurs in higher concentrations in the breast milk of women in third-world countries than in American women.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000044.subject: barium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000044.question: What is barium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000044.answer_short: Barium is a mineral Wallach counts among the body's essential nutrients, though most people know it from the 'barium meal' that lights up the gut on an X-ray.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000100.subject: barium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000100.question: Does barium build up in the body?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000100.answer_short: Yes — Wallach reports barium concentrates in hard tissues such as bone, and in the lung and eyes, and is thought to be essential to mammals.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000069.subject: barium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000069.question: Why do you have to drink barium before an X-ray?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000069.answer_short: Because barium sulfate is dense and blocks X-rays, it outlines the digestive tract on film — the basis of the 'barium meal' and 'barium enema.'

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000104.subject: neodymium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000104.question: What is neodymium?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000104.answer_short: Neodymium is a 'light' rare-earth trace mineral that Wallach says is proven to enhance normal cell growth and double the lifespan of laboratory species.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000259.subject: yttrium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000259.question: Does yttrium help you live longer?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000259.answer_short: Wallach reports that yttrium enhances normal cell growth and doubles the life span of laboratory species.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000260.subject: yttrium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000260.question: Does yttrium cross the placenta during pregnancy?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000260.answer_short: Wallach reports that yttrium rapidly crosses the placenta — about 14% of ingested yttrium can be detected in newborn mice.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000037.subject: arsenic
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000037.question: Can too little arsenic cause carpal tunnel syndrome?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000037.answer_short: Yes — Wallach holds that arsenic deficiency in humans shows up as carpal tunnel syndrome, TMJ and other repetitive-motion degenerative joint diseases.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000144.subject: arsenic
WAL-CLM-LETS-000144.question: What are the symptoms of arsenic poisoning?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000144.answer_short: Wallach lists arsenic-toxicity symptoms including hair loss, confusion, dermatitis, diarrhea, numbness, seizures and weakness, and says hair analysis is the best way to detect it.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000038.subject: arsenic
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000038.question: Can arsenic treat leukemia?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000038.answer_short: Wallach cites the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center that arsenic infusions work better than any other drug for certain types of leukemia.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000069.subject: tin
WAL-CLM-LETS-000069.question: How much tin should I take a day?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000069.answer_short: In Wallach's Base Line Nutritional Supplement Program, tin has a daily maintenance target of 500 mcg, with a 30-day pharmacologic dose of 1,000 mcg.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000249.subject: tin
WAL-CLM-RARE-000249.question: Does tin help prevent cancer?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000249.answer_short: Wallach cites evidence that tin has cancer-prevention properties and strongly induces the enzyme heme oxygenase, boosting heme breakdown in the kidney.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000248.subject: tin
WAL-CLM-RARE-000248.question: Does Wallach say humans need tin?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000248.answer_short: Yes -- Wallach holds that tin, once dismissed as mere tissue contamination, was proven by Schwarz's careful studies to be an essential trace element.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000097.subject: lutetium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000097.question: Is lutetium found in plants or in the body?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000097.answer_short: Yes -- Wallach's rare-earth data records lutetium occurring in land plants (up to 4.5 ppm) and in animal soft tissue and bone, not only in rocks and soil.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000216.subject: praseodymium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000216.question: What does praseodymium do in the body?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000216.answer_short: Wallach reports praseodymium enhances normal cell growth and doubled the life span of laboratory species.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000299.subject: titanium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000299.question: Where is titanium found in nature?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000299.answer_short: Wallach catalogs titanium across igneous rocks, soils, sea water, plants and animals, noting it accumulates in plankton.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000296.subject: scandium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000296.question: Does scandium accumulate in the body?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000296.answer_short: Yes — Wallach's mineral survey records that scandium, though present only in trace amounts, concentrates in mammalian heart and bone.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000295.subject: rhenium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000295.question: Does rhenium build up in the body?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000295.answer_short: Wallach records that land (terrestrial) animals accumulate rhenium in the thyroid, and catalogs its traces in rocks, marine plants and marine animals.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000085.subject: gadolinium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000085.question: What is gadolinium?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000085.answer_short: Gadolinium is a rare-earth mineral Wallach counts among the trace elements, found naturally in rocks, plants and animals.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000079.subject: dysprosium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000079.question: Where does the name dysprosium come from?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000079.answer_short: The name comes from the Greek word 'dysprositos,' meaning 'hard to get,' given by its discoverer after it was first identified in 1886.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000288.subject: dysprosium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000288.question: Does dysprosium build up in the body?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000288.answer_short: Wallach reports dysprosium occurs in terrestrial animals only in trace amounts (0.01 ppm), concentrated highest in the bones.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000251.subject: thulium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000251.question: Does thulium help you live longer?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000251.answer_short: Wallach reports that thulium supplementation enhances the growth of normal cells and has doubled the lifespans of laboratory species.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000247.subject: samarium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000247.question: Does samarium extend lifespan or help cells?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000247.answer_short: Wallach says samarium enhances normal cell proliferation and doubles the lifespan of laboratory species.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000261.subject: ytterbium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000261.question: Does ytterbium cross the placenta?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000261.answer_short: Yes -- Wallach reports ytterbium rapidly crosses the placenta, with 14% of an ingested amount detectable in newborn mice.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000297.subject: tantalum
WAL-CLM-RARE-000297.question: What is tantalum?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000297.answer_short: Tantalum (Ta) is a trace element Wallach catalogs among the rare, plant-derived minerals, distributed in nature from 2 ppm in igneous rocks down to trace levels.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000300.subject: zirconium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000300.question: Is zirconium found in plants and animals?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000300.answer_short: Yes -- Wallach's survey records zirconium in living tissue, about 20 ppm in marine plants and roughly 0.3 ppm in land animals, alongside rocks, soils and water.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000074.subject: cadmium
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000074.question: Does cadmium have any biological function in the body?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000074.answer_short: Despite being a toxic heavy metal, cadmium has real biological roles: it can substitute for zinc in zinc-deficient enzymes, it triggers the hatching of nematode (worm) cysts, and cadmium-bound proteins occur naturally in molluscs and horse kidney.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000143.subject: cadmium
WAL-CLM-RARE-000143.question: Is cadmium toxic, and what does it do in the body?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000143.answer_short: Wallach treats cadmium mainly as a toxic metal that builds up in the kidney and displaces four essential minerals — zinc, copper, calcium and selenium — from the enzymes that depend on them.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000061.subject: estrogen
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000061.question: Is estrogen therapy safe for osteoporosis?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000061.answer_short: Wallach opposes estrogen for osteoporosis: it can cause breast and uterine cancer, and he treats the disease as a mineral/absorption failure — betaine HCl, calcium, magnesium and colloidal minerals — not a hormone deficiency.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000091.subject: estrogen
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000091.question: Should you take estrogen during menopause?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000091.answer_short: Wallach advises against estrogen in menopause — it raises breast/uterine cancer risk — treating menopause as a normal transition to support: as the ovaries wind down, the adrenals and liver take over, aided by calcium, magnesium, diet and herbs.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000201.subject: hydrogen-peroxide
WAL-CLM-RARE-000201.question: How does food-grade hydrogen peroxide work as an oxygen therapy?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000201.answer_short: Wallach frames food-grade hydrogen peroxide as an oxygen therapy: diluted on an empty stomach or given IV, it's absorbed through the stomach and duodenal walls into the bloodstream, where it splits into water and singlet oxygen.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000202.subject: hydrogen-peroxide
WAL-CLM-RARE-000202.question: What has hydrogen peroxide therapy been used to treat?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000202.answer_short: Wallach says hydrogen peroxide has served as an oxygen therapy since the Civil War, and for 50+ years in Europe — for cancer, circulatory disease, emphysema, asthma and gangrene, and lately to revive dormant cells after a stroke.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000199.subject: hydrogen-peroxide
WAL-CLM-RARE-000199.question: How does the body use hydrogen peroxide to fight infection?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000199.answer_short: Wallach explains the body makes its own hydrogen peroxide: neutrophils produce it in organelles called peroxisomes to kill microbes, parasites and cancer cells, and the enzyme catalase breaks the excess into water and singlet oxygen.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000109.subject: arachidonic-acid
WAL-CLM-RARE-000109.question: Is arachidonic acid an essential fatty acid?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000109.answer_short: Arachidonic acid is usually counted among the essential fatty acids, but Wallach says only linoleic and linolenic truly are — the body can make arachidonic acid from linoleic acid, so it need not come from food.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000073.subject: ornithine
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000073.question: Does ornithine boost human growth hormone (HGH)?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000073.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says the amino acids L-arginine and ornithine can make the pituitary gland release HGH when supplemented in significant doses.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000444.subject: citrulline
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000444.question: How is citrulline related to arginine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000444.answer_short: Citrulline is the precursor the body converts into arginine, using the enzymes argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS) and argininosuccinate lyase (ASL).

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000445.subject: nitric-oxide
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000445.question: What does nitric oxide do, and how does the body make it?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000445.answer_short: Nitric oxide (NO) is made from the amino acid arginine; producing it lowers blood pressure and increases blood flow through obstructed blood vessels.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000446.subject: serotonin
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000446.question: What is serotonin?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000446.answer_short: A neurotransmitter the body makes from the amino acid tryptophan (via the enzyme tryptophan hydroxylase); it can then be converted onward into melatonin.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000447.subject: melatonin
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000447.question: What is melatonin?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000447.answer_short: A neurohormone the body makes from serotonin, which in turn comes from the amino acid tryptophan (tryptophan to serotonin to melatonin).

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000448.subject: coenzyme-a
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000448.question: What is coenzyme A and what does it do?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000448.answer_short: Coenzyme A is the active form of vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid) — it activates and transfers acyl groups, the reactions that release energy from carbohydrates, build and break down fatty acids, and make sterols, steroid hormones, and acetylcholine.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000449.subject: acetylcholine
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000449.question: What is acetylcholine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000449.answer_short: Acetylcholine is one of the body's most common neurotransmitters — the chemical nerve cells use to signal each other; the body builds it in the nervous system with choline as a structural component.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000450.subject: gamma-linolenic-acid
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000450.question: Is gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) an essential fatty acid?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000450.answer_short: An omega-6 fatty acid Wallach lists as "conditionally essential" — not strictly essential like linoleic and alpha-linolenic acid, but needed from the diet under certain conditions.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000451.subject: docosahexaenoic-acid
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000451.question: What is DHA and how is low DHA linked to depression?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000451.answer_short: An omega-3 fatty acid; Wallach says low blood DHA signals low brain 5-HIAA (a serotonin breakdown marker), which is directly tied to higher rates of depression and suicide.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000463.subject: nitrates
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000463.question: Are nitrates in processed meat bad for you?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000463.answer_short: Salt compounds added to cured meats and canned food to block bacteria and keep meat red; Wallach warns the stomach converts them into cancer-causing nitrosamines and they suppress the thyroid, making them a goitrogen.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000464.subject: nitrites
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000464.question: Are nitrites in bacon and cured meat bad for you?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000464.answer_short: Preservatives added with nitrates to cured meats to block bacteria and redden meat; Wallach warns the stomach converts them into cancer-causing nitrosamines, they suppress the thyroid, and he counts them as a dietary free radical to avoid.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000452.subject: arsenic-trioxide
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000452.question: Can arsenic be used to treat cancer?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000452.answer_short: Once a notorious poison, arsenic trioxide became an FDA-approved cancer drug in 2000; low doses put acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) patients into lasting remission.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000398.subject: tuna
WAL-CLM-RARE-000398.question: Does canned tuna contain lead, and is it safe to eat?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000398.answer_short: Wallach cites a study finding canned tuna carries nearly double the lead of fresh tuna — the lead leaches in from the sealant used to close the seams of steel and tin cans.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000288.subject: korsakoff
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000288.question: What is Korsakoff's syndrome?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000288.answer_short: Wallach's "false Alzheimer's": recent-memory loss driven by a vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency — often from alcoholism plus sugar — and reversible with high-dose thiamine.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000465.subject: berylliosis
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000465.question: What is berylliosis?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000465.answer_short: A painful, sometimes fatal lung disease caused by inhaling beryllium oxide dust from mining and industry; its chronic form resembles pulmonary sarcoidosis.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000399.subject: silver-nitrate
WAL-CLM-RARE-000399.question: What is silver nitrate (lunar caustic) and what has it been used for?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000399.answer_short: Silver nitrate, historically called 'lunar caustic,' has centuries of medicinal use — as a purgative, a cautery for wounds and tumors, and famously a 2% drop placed in newborns' eyes from 1884 to prevent gonorrheal blindness.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000289.subject: protein
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000289.question: What is the best quality protein?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000289.answer_short: Whole egg is the highest-quality protein Wallach lists — a chemical score of 100 and 94% utilization; animal proteins outrank plant proteins, and mixing plant sources fills in the missing amino acids.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000290.subject: testosterone
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000290.question: How can I raise my testosterone naturally?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000290.answer_short: Wallach's main lever for testosterone is the mineral boron — he says the body needs it to keep testosterone (and estrogen) at normal levels, and that supplementing boron doubles testosterone.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000014.subject: korsakoff
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000014.question: Can Korsakoff's syndrome be reversed?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000014.answer_short: Yes — Wallach places Korsakoff's syndrome in the Beriberi (vitamin B1 deficiency) family and holds it reversible by cutting sugar, fried foods, processed meats, oils and gluten and supplying all 90 essential nutrients with extra thiamine.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000015.subject: korsakoff
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000015.question: What is Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000015.answer_short: Wallach's 'third dementia': a two-part syndrome in which a patient has both Korsakoff's syndrome and multiple sclerosis at once — reversed by treating both, with 6-8 eggs a day to rebuild the brain's myelin plus all 90 nutrients and antioxidants like selenium.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000333.subject: korsakoff
WAL-CLM-LETS-000333.question: How does Wallach treat Korsakoff's syndrome?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000333.answer_short: Wallach's Korsakoff protocol: IV chelation and IV hydrogen peroxide, vitamin B1 100 mg 3x/day, lecithin 2,500 mg 3x/day, no alcohol or sugar, chromium/vanadium, betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes, plus the nootropics hydergine, vasopressin nasal spray, centrophenoxine and piracetam.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000291.subject: testosterone
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000291.question: Do you need cholesterol to make testosterone?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000291.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says the body builds testosterone out of cholesterol, and warns that driving cholesterol too low can leave a man 'totally disinterested in sex.'

WAL-CLM-RARE-000400.subject: testosterone
WAL-CLM-RARE-000400.question: Does testosterone cause teenage violence or aggression?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000400.answer_short: Wallach argues the puberty testosterone surge (ages 14–18), landing on top of mineral deficiencies and a high-sugar diet, is an 'explosive' driver of teen crime and murder.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000292.subject: testosterone
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000292.question: Does Wallach recommend taking testosterone for impotence or low libido?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000292.answer_short: Yes — among his impotence remedies Wallach lists 'oral testosterone,' which he specifies as glandular food supplements plus testosterone by injection (IM), alongside herbs like ginseng and saw palmetto.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000293.subject: korsakoff
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000293.question: Has Wallach's memory-loss treatment actually restored anyone's memory?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000293.answer_short: Yes — Wallach cites his multi-drug Korsakoff protocol (nootropics like centrophenoxine and piracetam, plus IV chelation, vitamin B1, lecithin and chromium/vanadium) as the exact program used to restore the memory of Princess Diana's bodyguard.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000453.subject: korsakoff
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000453.question: Why does Wallach call Korsakoff's syndrome 'cerebral beriberi'?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000453.answer_short: Because he classifies it as beriberi — thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency — striking the brain; he groups it with MS, ALS, Alzheimer's and Creutzfeld-Jakob as brain-lesion diseases that share a broad symptom list.
